html.question: What is semantic HTML?
html.answer: Semantic HTML uses tags that describe their meaning rather than only their appearance — header, nav, main, article, section, aside and footer. It improves accessibility for screen readers and helps search engines understand the page structure, while also making the code easier to read for other developers. Semantic tags are not a display mode: some are block-level (e.g. <header>, <main>, <section>) and some are inline (e.g. <strong>, <em>), so "semantic" says what the element means, never how it is displayed. The accessibility payoff is concrete rather than general: assistive technology exposes header, nav and main as landmarks, so a user can jump between regions and straight to the content instead of tabbing through everything - and a skip link works for the same reason, because it can target main. Headings build an outline that can be navigated by level, and a native element such as button, label or table already carries its role, keyboard behaviour and state. The trap is replacing those with divs and spans: the browser then announces generic text with no role, no keyboard support and no state, and rebuilding that by hand with roles and tabindex is more work and usually less correct than having used the right element in the first place.

html.question: What is the difference between a div and a span?
html.answer: A div is a block-level container that takes the full available width and starts on a new line, while a span is an inline container that flows inside a line of text. Use a div to group larger layout blocks and a span to style or group a fragment of text without breaking the line.

examples.title: block vs inline vs span
examples.code: AB
examples.explanation: div is block-level, so it breaks the line and stretches; spans sit side by side inside the surrounding text.

html.question: When should I use a class instead of an id?
html.answer: An id must be unique on the page and is used when you need to identify a single element — for example as an anchor, or a CSS selector that definitely targets one node. A class can be reused across many elements, so if a style or behaviour applies to more than one element, prefer a class.

examples.title: id for one node, class for many
examples.code:
Sale
new beta
examples.explanation: The id must be unique and is what fragment links (#main-banner) and JS lookups use; the class is the reusable hook.

html.question: How do I make an image render well on different screen sizes?
html.answer: A box only keeps an image's proportions if you tell it the ratio up front, and there are two ways. The classic technique is the padding hack: wrap the image in a container whose padding-bottom is the height divided by the width as a percentage (56.25% for a 16:9 image), and absolutely position the image to fill that box - because the padding is calculated from the container's width, the ratio holds before the image has loaded. The modern replacement is the CSS aspect-ratio property: set aspect-ratio on the element and it strictly respects the original image ratio, with no wrapper and no absolute positioning. If you are designing for modern browsers, skip the padding hack and use aspect-ratio.

examples.title: The padding hack
examples.explanation: A percentage padding-bottom is resolved against the container's width, so the box holds a 16:9 ratio before the image arrives; the image is absolutely positioned to fill it.

examples.title: Modern CSS aspect-ratio (skip the hack)
examples.explanation: aspect-ratio does the padding hack's job with no wrapper and no absolute positioning; for modern browsers you can skip the padding hack entirely.

html.question: Why is the alt attribute important on images?
html.answer: The alt attribute provides a text alternative that is announced by screen readers and shown when the image fails to load. It is required when the image conveys information, and should describe the content or purpose. Decorative images can use an empty alt="", but hiding them without an attribute hurts accessibility.

examples.title: Meaningful vs decorative alt
examples.explanation: Describe the information for content images; use alt="" for decoration so it is skipped, and never omit alt for meaningful images.

html.question: How do I show a block of code on a page?
html.answer: Wrap the lines in pre/code tags to keep whitespace and line breaks intact. Escape raw angle brackets as < and > inside the block, and add overflow-x: auto so long lines scroll horizontally instead of breaking the layout.

examples.title: Code block that survives long lines
examples.code:
const total = items
  .filter(i => i.active)
  .reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0);
examples.explanation: pre keeps whitespace and newlines, escaped < > stop the browser parsing tags, and overflow-x keeps one long line from breaking the layout.

html.question: What is the difference between <article> and <section>?
html.answer: <article> is a self-contained composition that makes sense on its own - a blog post, a news story, a comment - and could be syndicated or reused independently. <section> is a thematic grouping of related content within a page, usually with a heading. Use section to break up a long page, article for content that stands alone; an article can contain sections.

examples.title: <article> vs <section>
examples.code:
Blog Post

Intro

...
examples.explanation: article is standalone/reusable; section groups related content with a heading.

html.question: How do you correctly associate a <label> with a form control?
html.answer: Give the control an id and point the label's for attribute at it, or nest the control inside the label. The association means clicking the label focuses/activates the control and screen readers announce the label text. A placeholder attribute is not a substitute - it disappears when the user types and is poorly announced.

examples.title: Label association
examples.code:
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email">

<!-- or nested -->
<label>Email <input type="email"></label>
examples.explanation: Use for+id or nesting for accessibility and click-to-focus.

html.question: What is the difference between async and defer on a <script> tag?
html.answer: Both are boolean attributes that let an external script download without blocking HTML parsing; the difference is when it executes. defer downloads in parallel and executes once the document has been parsed, in order, right before DOMContentLoaded - reliable for scripts that touch the DOM. async downloads in parallel and executes as soon as it is ready, which can interrupt parsing and ignores order - fine for independent analytics but unsafe for scripts that depend on each other. Neither blocks parsing, but only defer preserves execution order.

examples.title: async vs defer
examples.code:
<!-- executes as soon as loaded, order not guaranteed -->
<script async src="analytics.js"></script>

<!-- executes after parsing, in order -->
<script defer src="vendor.js"></script>
<script defer src="app.js"></script>
examples.explanation: defer preserves execution order and runs before DOMContentLoaded.

html.question: What is the viewport meta tag and why does it matter on mobile?
html.answer: <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'> tells the browser to render at the device width instead of a desktop-width virtual viewport. Without it, mobile browsers zoom out to fit a desktop layout, making text tiny and tap targets hard to hit. It is the HTML precondition for responsive CSS to work.

examples.title: Viewport meta
examples.code: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
examples.explanation: Ensures mobile renders at device width for responsive layouts.

html.question: What is the difference between <strong>/<em> and <b>/<i>?
html.answer: <strong> and <em> carry meaning: strong implies importance (read as emphasis by screen readers, often bold), em adds stress emphasis (often italic). <b> and <i> are purely presentational - b is bold text, i is italic text - and pass no semantic meaning. Prefer the semantic pair and style them with CSS; reserve b/i for purely visual effects.

examples.title: Semantic vs presentational
examples.code:
This is important and emphasized.

This is bold and italic.
examples.explanation: strong/em carry meaning; b/i are purely visual.

html.question: How does native browser form validation work and when would you disable it?
html.answer: Constraints like required, type='email', min/max length and the pattern attribute are validated by the browser: the form is blocked from submitting and the :invalid pseudo-class lets you style errors. Setting novalidate (or noValidate) on the form disables native bubbles so you can run your own validation - useful when you need consistent messaging or server-side rules.

examples.title: Form validation
examples.code:
<form novalidate (ngSubmit)="submit()">
  <input required type="email">
  <button>Submit</button>
</form>
examples.explanation: novalidate disables native validation for custom error handling.

html.question: How do you put audio and video on a page, and what do you have to get right?
html.answer: The browser gives you this natively: video and audio elements take one or more source children with a type, plus fallback content for anything that cannot play them - no plugins, no player library required for the basics. What separates a working embed from a correct one is the list around the media itself. Accessibility first: captions for pre-recorded speech (a track with kind=captions), a transcript for audio, and controls left on so keyboard users have play, seek and volume without hunting for a custom widget; autoplay only ever with muted and playsinline, and even then only when it cannot be avoided. Performance next: poster for the first frame, preload=none when the video is below the fold, and lazy-load it like any other heavy asset rather than letting the page fetch a 20 MB file it may never show. Then the practicalities - MP4/H.264 is still the safe default, WebM where you want open codecs and smaller files, know that codecs differ by browser, and long or adaptive content wants streaming (HLS with a player or native support) rather than a giant file. Responsive is the least of it: width:100% plus an aspect-ratio box handles layout.

examples.title: A captioned, non-blocking video
examples.explanation: preload=none and the poster keep it off the critical path until the user acts, the captions track makes it usable without sound, and the fallback link covers both an unsupported browser and a failed download.

html.question: How does native drag and drop work in HTML, and how would you build it in Angular?
html.answer: HTML gives you drag and drop natively. Mark the source draggable="true" and handle dragstart on it, then handle dragover and drop on the target. Only one detail trips people up: the target must call preventDefault() in dragover, otherwise the browser assumes the default action and drop never fires. The payload travels through event.dataTransfer - setData in dragstart, getData in drop. In Angular those are just event bindings, and for a real feature such as reordering a list, moving cards between Kanban columns or a file drop zone, I would use the Angular CDK's cdkDrag and cdkDropList instead of hand-rolling the index maths. The part not to skip is accessibility: native drag and drop does not work for keyboard or screen-reader users, so every drag action needs an equivalent - Move up/down buttons or a menu action - with clear labels and an announcement when the order changes.

examples.title: The template
examples.code:
Drag me
Drop here
examples.explanation: draggable on the source, and the inline preventDefault in dragover is what allows the drop - remove that one call and drop never fires.

examples.title: The handlers
examples.explanation: setData in dragstart and getData in drop: the payload is carried as text/plain data, so you move an identifier rather than markup.

html.question: What is the difference between SVG and Canvas, and when would you use each?
html.answer: SVG and Canvas mostly differ in what they are made of. SVG is a document: every shape is a real DOM element you can style with CSS, select, focus, animate and attach a listener to, it stays sharp at any zoom or print size, and it sits in the accessibility tree, where you can give it a role, a title and a description. Its limit is node count - a chart drawn as ten thousand SVG paths is ten thousand objects for the browser to lay out and for Angular to track. Canvas is the opposite: a single element and a bitmap surface you paint yourself. You ask for a context (2d, or webgl when you want the GPU), issue imperative drawing commands such as fillRect, arc, lineTo and drawImage, and then clear and redraw whenever something changes, usually inside a requestAnimationFrame loop. That makes it the right tool at volume and for pixel work: tens of thousands of moving points, games and animation loops, image filters and cropping, heatmaps, signature pads. The trade-offs are the point of the answer: because there are no elements, CSS styling and per-shape events do not exist - hover and click are hit-testing maths you write yourself with isPointInPath or a distance check; nothing on the surface is in the accessibility tree, so give the canvas role=img and an accessible name, or publish the same data as text or a table next to it; you handle devicePixelRatio yourself or it looks blurry on a retina display; and exporting means toDataURL rather than reading the DOM. My rule: choose by interaction and accessibility first, then by volume - anything the user inspects, selects, hovers or reads should be SVG, and anything with thousands of repainted objects or pixel-level manipulation should be Canvas. In Angular that is inline SVG in the template, and Canvas behind a ViewChild with its drawing loop stopped in ngOnDestroy.

examples.title: The accessibility difference in five lines
examples.code:
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 40" role="img" aria-labelledby="title">
  <title id="title">Revenue up 18% this quarter</title>
  <path d="M0 35 L40 28 L70 15 L100 5" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" />
</svg>

<canvas width="400" height="160" role="img"
  aria-label="Revenue up 18% this quarter"></canvas>
examples.explanation: The SVG carries a real title element and a stroke the browser renders crisply at any zoom; the canvas carries only the label you give it, because everything drawn into it is invisible to the accessibility tree.

examples.title: What a canvas actually is
examples.explanation: One element, one surface: repainting everything each frame is cheap at tens of thousands of points, but hover, focus and clicks are maths you write, and the DOM has no idea what is on screen.

html.question: What are the different ways to hide an element, and what does each mean for layout and accessibility?
html.answer: There are several, and they are not interchangeable - the right one depends on whether you care about layout space, focusability or what assistive technology announces. display:none (or the hidden attribute, which is a UA rule for exactly that) removes the element from layout and from the accessibility tree entirely: nothing is painted, nothing takes space, nothing is announced, and on Angular it is what @if produces when the branch is removed from the DOM. visibility:hidden keeps the box and its space but hides the painting and still removes it from the accessibility tree, which is what you want for a reserved placeholder that must not be read. opacity:0 is the trap: the element is invisible but still there - it can still be clicked, still be tabbed to, and screen readers may still reach it - so pairing it with inert or pointer-events:none is mandatory if it is meant to be inactive. aria-hidden only hides it from assistive technology while leaving it visible and, dangerously, still focusable, which creates the classic focus-into-invisible-content bug. The modern, honest option is the inert attribute: it removes the subtree from focus, from interaction and from the accessibility tree at once. In Angular I reach for @if when losing and recreating the DOM is fine, and a binding to [hidden] or [inert] when the component must keep its state - and I always check the tab order afterwards.

examples.title: Three toggles, three different meanings
examples.code:
@if (open()) { }
Draft: {{ draft() }}
{{ panelContent() }}
examples.explanation: @if trades state for absence, [hidden] keeps state but not focusability, [inert] keeps state and blocks focus - and opacity:0 would do none of these, which is why it is the one to avoid as a visibility toggle.

html.question: What values can the type attribute of an input take, and what do they actually give you?
html.answer: The type attribute chooses which control the browser renders, and with it the keyboard a mobile user gets, the browser's own validation and the shape of the value you read back. The practical set falls into groups. Text-shaped: text (the default), password, email, url, search, and tel - which has no format rule of its own, because phone numbers differ by country. Numeric: number, which brings a spinner, arrow-key stepping and native min/max/step validation, with the caveat that it also refuses non-numeric characters and handles locale decimal separators inconsistently, so for an id-like or phone-like field inputmode is the better tool; and range for a slider. Temporal: date, time, datetime-local, month and week, which give a native picker where the browser supports it. Choice and binary: checkbox, radio (grouped by name), and file with accept and multiple. Submitter plumbing: submit, reset, button, image and hidden. Two details worth stating out loud: an unrecognised type degrades to text rather than breaking the page, which is what makes the attribute safe to use, and type is only part of the decision - inputmode picks the keyboard, autocomplete lets the browser fill the field, and enterkeyhint labels the key. Choose by the intent of the data and let the browser do work you would otherwise write by hand.

examples.title: The same form, letting the browser carry the semantics
examples.code:
<form (ngSubmit)="save()">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required />

  <label for="phone">Phone</label>
  <!-- tel has no format rule; inputmode gets the numeric keypad anyway -->
  <input id="phone" name="phone" type="tel" inputmode="tel" autocomplete="tel" />

  <label for="salary">Expected salary</label>
  <input id="salary" name="salary" type="number" min="0" step="1000" />

  <label for="start">Start date</label>
  <input id="start" name="start" type="date" />

  <label for="cv">CV</label>
  <input id="cv" name="cv" type="file" accept=".pdf,.docx" />

  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
examples.explanation: email and date are validated and rendered by the browser, tel borrows the numeric keypad without pretending to validate, and type=submit is what makes Enter work as the user expects. In Angular the value is bound like any attribute, so [type] works - but these give you validation and keyboard for free that no amount of TypeScript can.

css.question: What is the CSS box model?
css.answer: Every element is rendered as a box made of four layers, from the inside out: content, padding, border and margin. Content holds the actual content, padding adds space between content and border, the border frames the box, and margin creates space between this box and its neighbours. box-sizing: border-box makes width and height include padding and border: because the declared width now measures the border box, the content area shrinks to leave room for that padding and border instead of the element growing past the width you set. Margin sits outside the box and is never part of box-sizing.

examples.title: Box model with content-box vs border-box
examples.explanation: content-box measures only the content; border-box makes width/height include padding and border, which is why global resets set it.

css.question: What is the difference between padding and margin?
css.answer: Padding is the space inside the element, between the content and the border. Margin is the space outside the element, between the border and neighbouring elements. Padding is always part of the element's background; margins collapse with adjacent margins.

examples.title: Padding is inside, margin is outside
examples.explanation: Padding grows the element and shows its background; margin separates elements and can collapse with an adjacent margin.

css.question: What is the difference between block, inline and inline-block?
css.answer: Block elements start on a new line and fill the available width. Inline elements flow within a line of text and ignore width and height. Inline-block flows inline but respects width, height and vertical margins like a block, which makes it useful for grid-like layouts.

examples.title: block
examples.code: .header { display: block; }  /* full width, own line */
examples.explanation: The default for div, p, section - takes the available width and starts a new line.

examples.title: inline
examples.code: .tag { display: inline; }   /* width/height ignored, stays in the line */
examples.explanation: The default for span, a, strong - flows with the surrounding text.

examples.title: inline-block
examples.code: .badge { display: inline-block; width: 80px; height: 24px; }
examples.explanation: Flows inline but respects width, height and vertical margin - a building block for chip/button rows.

css.question: What do align-items and justify-content do in flexbox?
css.answer: justify-content controls the distribution of items along the main axis (the flex container's flex-direction). align-items controls alignment along the cross axis, which is perpendicular to the main axis. For a default row layout, justify-content is horizontal and align-items is vertical.

examples.title: Row vs column flexbox
examples.code:
.row  { display: flex; flex-direction: row;            justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; }
.col  { display: flex; flex-direction: column;         justify-content: space-between; align-items: stretch; }
examples.explanation: justify-content works along flex-direction (main axis), align-items across it (cross axis) - swap the two when you switch direction.

css.question: How do you center a block element horizontally?
css.answer: Give the element a width and set margin-inline: auto (or margin-left and margin-right to auto). The auto margins split the remaining space equally on both sides. Flexbox centers with display: flex and justify-content: center for a row of items.

examples.title: Centering with auto margins
examples.code: .box { width: 300px; margin-inline: auto; }  /* splits leftover space evenly */
examples.explanation: Works for a single block element with a known width.

examples.title: Centering with flexbox
examples.code:
.wrapper { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; height: 100vh; }
.centered { width: 300px; }
examples.explanation: Centres both axes without knowing the size, and works for any number of children.

css.question: What are specificity and the cascade, and where does !important fit in?
css.answer: The cascade decides which rule wins when selectors conflict; specificity ranks them by id (highest), then class/attribute/pseudo-class, then type selectors, and a style attribute beats all of those normal author rules. !important lifts an author declaration above every normal author rule, including the style attribute, which is why it is a code smell: the only thing that reliably beats it is another !important, so the source of a style becomes unpredictable. Prefer increasing specificity or changing the order and origin of the stylesheet instead.

examples.title: Specificity example
examples.explanation: Cascade + specificity decide; !important breaks the normal order, and the only escape from it is another !important.

examples.title: Where pseudo-class, attribute and type selectors rank
examples.explanation: A pseudo-class (:hover), an attribute selector ([type=text]) and a class each count 0,1,0 - above type selectors, below an id. The later of two equal rules wins.

css.question: What are CSS custom properties (variables) and how are themes built with them?
css.answer: Custom properties are defined on a selector with --name and read with var(--name). They cascade and can be redefined on a themed container, which is how theming works: define --primary, --bg and --text on :root, then override them on a .dark or [data-theme='dark'] selector. Because they cascade, a component can read var(--primary) and automatically adapt to whichever theme is active.

examples.title: CSS variables for theming
examples.explanation: Redefining on a container/theme selector cascades to all children.

examples.title: Toggling the theme from HTML
examples.code:
<html data-theme="light">
  <body>
    <button (click)="toggleTheme()">Toggle theme</button>
  </body>
</html>

// toggleTheme() flips one attribute:
// document.documentElement.dataset.theme = 'dark'
examples.explanation: Because the variables are redefined under [data-theme='dark'], flipping that single attribute re-themes every element that reads var(--bg) or var(--text).

css.question: What is the difference between position: relative, absolute, fixed and sticky?
css.answer: relative offsets an element from its normal flow position without removing it from flow. absolute takes the element out of flow and positions it relative to the nearest positioned ancestor (a relative/absolute parent); without one, relative to the containing block. fixed positions it relative to the viewport, so it stays put while scrolling. sticky toggles between relative and fixed as the element crosses a scroll threshold - useful for section headers.

examples.title: Positioning
examples.explanation: absolute relative to nearest positioned ancestor; sticky toggles on scroll.

css.question: What are responsive breakpoints and why is mobile-first preferable?
css.answer: Breakpoints are viewport widths where the layout changes, defined with media queries (@media (min-width: 768px)). Mobile-first means you write the base styles for small screens and layer on wider layouts with min-width queries, so narrow devices get less CSS and no override churn. Because min-width is additive, wide screens upgrade rather than narrow screens override.

examples.title: Mobile-first
examples.code:
/* base mobile */ .grid { display: block; }
/* tablet+ */ @media (min-width: 768px) { .grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; } }
examples.explanation: min-width queries add layout as viewport grows.

css.question: What is the difference between px, rem, em, % and vw/vh?
css.answer: px is a fixed unit; rem is relative to the root font-size (so 2rem scales with the user's base size and stays predictable); em is relative to the element's own font-size and compounds as it nests; % is relative to the parent's size for the same property; vw/vh are 1% of viewport width/height. Prefer rem for spacing and text so zoom and browser font settings work, and %/flex units for layout.

examples.title: Units
examples.code:
html { font-size: 16px; }
.card { padding: 1rem; /* 16px */ margin: 0.5em; /* relative to current font */ width: 50%; height: 50vh; }
examples.explanation: rem predictable for spacing; em compounds; % parent-based; vh/vw viewport-based.

css.question: When would you use CSS Grid and when Flexbox?
css.answer: Grid is two-dimensional - it sizes and positions items across explicit rows and columns, ideal for page layouts, card grids and dashboards. Flexbox is one-dimensional - it distributes items along a single axis, ideal for navbars, aligning rows, centering and wrapping lists. Modern usage: Grid for the big layout skeleton, Flexbox for everyday alignment inside cells; they compose, not compete.

examples.title: Grid vs Flexbox
examples.code:
.layout { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr; gap: 1rem; }
.nav { display: flex; gap: .5rem; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; }
examples.explanation: Grid 2D layout skeleton; Flexbox 1D alignment.

css.question: What problems do global styles cause, and how do you keep styles contained?
css.answer: Global styles fail quietly: a rule written for one screen silently restyles every element that matches it in another screen, and the symptom appears three features later as a button that is the wrong height. The usual categories are selector collisions, specificity fights between files loaded in an order nobody controls, inherited properties leaking somewhere they were not wanted, third-party styles overriding yours (or yours breaking a library), and design drift, where spacing and colour are re-decided per screen because nothing forces them to be shared. Angular's default emulated view encapsulation scopes component styles to that component - they are rewritten with content attributes so they cannot match anything else - which is the containment mechanism I lean on, so the global file stays small. My rules: globals hold only the reset, design tokens as CSS custom properties, base typography and genuinely shared primitives; feature styling lives with the component; avoid bare element selectors and generic classes like .container in globals; use cascade layers when a library and your own styles need an explicit order; use !important only as a last resort with a comment; and reach for ViewEncapsulation.None deliberately, for something like a third-party theme, rather than by accident. The test is simple - if a change in one component's styles alters another component's pixels, containment has failed.

examples.title: What belongs in globals versus with the component
examples.explanation: The global file defines the vocabulary once; components spend it through var(). A rule that only one component needs is scoped to that component, so it cannot be inherited by accident anywhere else.

javascript.question: What is hoisting in JavaScript, and how does it differ for var, let and const?
javascript.answer: Hoisting is the default behaviour where declarations are processed before any code runs, so the engine "knows" about them at the top of the scope. var declarations (and function declarations) are hoisted and initialised to undefined, so reading them before the line throws nothing - you get undefined. let and const are hoisted too but stay in the temporal dead zone until the declaration executes, so accessing them earlier throws a ReferenceError. Hoisting applies to the declaration, not the assignment.

examples.title: var vs let before declaration
examples.explanation: var is initialised to undefined at scope start; let/const live in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs.

javascript.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
javascript.answer: var is function-scoped, hoisted, and can be redeclared - the source of most closure bugs in loops. let is block-scoped, hoisted but not initialised, and cannot be redeclared in the same block, so it is the default choice. const is also block-scoped and cannot be reassigned after initialisation, but note it does not make the value immutable - a const object can still have its properties changed.

examples.title: Loop scoping bug
examples.code:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // 3, 3, 3
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // 0, 1, 2
examples.explanation: var shares one binding across the whole function; let creates a new binding per iteration.

examples.title: const is not deeply immutable
examples.explanation: const freezes the binding, not the value inside it.

javascript.question: What is a closure?
javascript.answer: A closure is the combination of a function with its lexical environment: an inner function keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that outer function has returned. That is how private state, memoisation caches and event handlers that remember their context work.

examples.title: Counter with private state
examples.explanation: count survives after createCounter returned because the returned functions captured its scope.

javascript.question: What is the difference between null and undefined?
javascript.answer: undefined means a value has never been assigned - missing arguments, absent properties, uninitialised lets, and the return value of a function with no return. null is an explicit signal from the developer that there is intentionally no value. In practice: use undefined for absence by default, null to say "deliberately empty", and prefer ?? over || so 0 and empty string are not swallowed.

examples.title: ?? vs ||
examples.code:
0 || 'fallback';   // 'fallback'  (0 is falsy)
0 ?? 'fallback';   // 0          (only null/undefined fall through)
examples.explanation: || treats every falsy value as missing; ?? only treats null and undefined as missing.

javascript.question: What are arrow functions and how do they differ from function declarations?
javascript.answer: An arrow function is the shorter way to write a function that arrived in ES6: const add = (a, b) => a + b, with the parentheses around a single parameter optional and the return keyword dropped when the body is one expression. The difference that matters in interviews is this: an arrow function has no this of its own. A normal function gets this from how it is called - user.greetRegular() makes this the user object - while an arrow function inherits this from the scope it was written in, so calling it as a method cannot change it. That is why arrows are the right choice for map, filter and callbacks, and the wrong choice for an object method that needs this to be the object. Two smaller differences come from the same place: an arrow has no arguments object, so use rest parameters instead, and it cannot be used with new because it has no prototype, so it is never a constructor. Because an arrow is usually assigned to a const, it cannot be hoisted and called before that line the way a function declaration can.

examples.title: this in a regular function vs an arrow function
examples.explanation: A regular method reads this from the call site, so user.greetRegular() hands it the object. An arrow ignores the call site and keeps the this of the surrounding scope, which here is the module scope - so this.name is undefined even though it was called on user.

examples.title: An arrow defined inside a method keeps that method's this
examples.explanation: The arrow is written inside greet, so it takes greet's this, and greet's this is user because the method was called on user. The inner regular function is a new function with a fresh this from its own call, and regular() is not user.regular(), so in strict mode it is undefined.

examples.title: No arguments object, and not a constructor
examples.explanation: Arrows have no arguments object and no prototype, so they cannot be newed and cannot be constructors - a rest parameter and a normal function replace both.

javascript.question: What is the difference between a function and a method?
javascript.answer: A function is a standalone callable, usually declared at module scope and invoked by name. A method is a function that lives on an object and is invoked as obj.method(), so it receives the object as this. The same function object can be used either way - what changes is how it is called and therefore what this is. A standalone function that does not use this at all is better described as a plain function, not a method.

examples.title: Same function, two call styles
examples.explanation: A function becomes a method through its call site, which supplies this.

javascript.question: What is event propagation, and what are the capture and bubble phases?
javascript.answer: Event propagation is the process by which an event travels through the DOM tree to determine which element's listeners fire and in what order. It has three phases. Capturing (the trickle-down): the event starts at the root — window/document — and travels down through every ancestor until it reaches the target. Target: the event arrives at the element that was actually triggered (event.target) and the listeners attached directly to it run. Bubbling (floating up): the event reverses and travels back up from the target through its parents and ancestors to the root, which is where most listeners run. addEventListener accepts a third argument - true registers in the capture phase, false (the default) or omitted registers in the bubble phase.

examples.title: Listening in each phase
examples.code:
document.addEventListener('click', log, true);  // capture: root first
button.addEventListener('click', log);      // target
panel.addEventListener('click', log);       // bubble: nearest ancestor first

function log(e) { console.log(e.eventPhase, e.currentTarget); }
examples.explanation: The same handler can observe the event at three different points in its path.

javascript.question: What is the difference between event.preventDefault() and event.stopPropagation()?
javascript.answer: preventDefault() cancels the default browser action for that event - following a link, submitting a form, checking a checkbox - but the event still travels to other listeners. stopPropagation() stops the event from reaching any further nodes, so ancestor and descendant handlers never run; the default action still happens unless you also call preventDefault(). stopImmediatePropagation() additionally prevents the remaining listeners on the same element.

examples.title: One is not the other
examples.explanation: preventDefault changes what the browser does; stopPropagation changes who else hears about it.

javascript.question: What are the common array methods - map, filter, reduce, forEach - and when do you use each?
javascript.answer: forEach runs a side effect per element and returns undefined - never use it to build a new array. map returns a new array of the same length with each element transformed. filter returns a new array of only the elements that pass a test. reduce folds the array into one value (sum, group, object) and always returns an accumulator you must initialise. Prefer these over raw for loops when you only need a transformation; use .at(), .find(), .some(), .every() and .sort() for the other common cases.

examples.title: The four shapes
examples.code:
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];

nums.forEach(n => log(n));                  // side effect only
const doubled = nums.map(n => n * 2);      // [2, 4, 6, 8]
const evens = nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);// [2, 4]
const total = nums.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0); // 10
examples.explanation: Each operator has a distinct job; mixing them up usually means you wanted a different one.

examples.title: Grouping with reduce
examples.explanation: reduce is the general-purpose fold - handy for grouping, counting and building lookups.

javascript.question: What is the spread operator, and how is it different from rest parameters?
javascript.answer: Spread (...) expands an iterable into individual elements or properties at the call site - used to copy arrays/objects and to pass an array as separate arguments. Rest parameters collect an indefinite number of arguments passed to a function into a real array, and must be the last parameter in the definition; rest in destructuring gathers the remaining properties into an object. They use the same three dots but sit in opposite positions: spread produces many values from one, rest collects many values into one.

examples.title: Both directions
examples.explanation: Spread spreads out, rest gathers in.

examples.title: Rest parameters bundle arguments into an array
examples.explanation: ...numbers is a true array, so array methods work on it directly - unlike the old arguments object.

examples.title: Positional parameters plus rest
examples.explanation: The rest parameter must come last; it takes everything the earlier named parameters did not.

javascript.question: What are Map, Set and WeakMap, and how do they differ from plain objects and arrays?
javascript.answer: Set holds unique values with fast has/add and preserves insertion order. Map holds key-value pairs with a typed API and reliable iteration, and unlike an object it accepts any value as a key and exposes size, keys(), values() and entries(). WeakMap is the non-enumerable, garbage-collectable variant of Map: keys must be objects and entries vanish when the key is unreachable, which is why it is used for private per-object caches. Use a Set for membership tests instead of indexOf on an array.

examples.title: Membership and lookup
examples.explanation: Collections give O(1) lookups and safe handling of keys that objects cannot express.

examples.title: WeakMap for private per-object state
examples.explanation: Because the keys are objects, entries are collected once the nodes become unreachable.

javascript.question: Why is JavaScript single-threaded, and how can it still handle concurrent work?
javascript.answer: One thread plus one synchronous call stack means code cannot interleave mid-statement, so you never get data races on shared memory - which is why it is safe by default. Concurrency comes from the event loop: the stack runs to completion, then the microtask queue (promise callbacks) is drained, then one macrotask (timers, I/O callbacks) is processed. I/O is delegated to the browser or Node, so while a request is in flight the main thread is free. That is also why a long synchronous loop freezes the UI - and why heavy work goes to a Web Worker.

examples.title: Order of execution
examples.explanation: All synchronous code runs first, then microtasks, then the next macrotask.

javascript.question: What is the prototype chain?
javascript.answer: Prototypes are the mechanism by which JavaScript objects inherit features from one another. Every object has a built-in property, its prototype (the internal [[Prototype]] link), and the prototype is itself an object with its own prototype - so property lookup walks a chain and stops only when it reaches a prototype whose own prototype is null. That is how arrays inherit from Array.prototype, functions from Function.prototype, and how any object can delegate shared behaviour to another: "inheritance" in JavaScript is delegation along the chain, not copying. Object.create(proto) sets the link directly, Object.getPrototypeOf reads it, and class syntax is sugar over the same mechanism.

examples.title: Properties are found along the chain
examples.explanation: greet() is the object's own property; toString() is found further up the chain, which is why you can call methods you never wrote.

examples.title: Manual delegation
examples.explanation: Properties are looked up along the chain, so shared behaviour lives on one shared object.

javascript.question: What do call, apply and bind do?
javascript.answer: All three change what this refers to when a function is invoked. call invokes the function immediately with the given this and arguments listed individually. apply invokes it immediately with an array-like list of arguments. bind returns a new function with this permanently bound and arguments partially applied - which is how you keep a handler working when you pass it to addEventListener.

examples.title: Invocation styles
examples.explanation: call/apply run now; bind produces a reusable function with this fixed.

examples.title: Video walkthrough
examples.code: call, apply and bind - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=75W8UPQ5l7k
examples.explanation: A short visual run through setting this with call, apply and bind, and why bind is the one that returns a new function instead of calling immediately.

javascript.question: What does use strict do?
javascript.answer: It opts a script or function into strict mode, which removes the sloppy-mode escape hatches: undeclared assignments throw instead of creating a global, this inside a plain function call is undefined rather than the global object, duplicate parameters are rejected, and writes to non-writable properties throw instead of failing silently. Modules and class bodies are always strict, so bundler-based Angular code is strict whether you ask for it or not.

examples.title: Errors instead of silent globals
examples.explanation: Strict mode converts silent misbehaviour into immediate errors.

javascript.question: What are the ES6+ features worth knowing as an Angular developer?
javascript.answer: The ones you meet daily: let/const with block scoping, arrow functions, template literals, destructuring with defaults and rest, spread for copying, classes, ES modules with import/export, and the null-handling operators ?. and ??. Map/Set replaced the need for most object-as-dictionary hacks, and Object.entries/values/fromEntries make transformation easy. Later editions add optional catch binding, logical assignment (??=, ||=) and Array.prototype.at for negative indexing.

examples.title: Everyday uses
examples.code:
const state = { user: { name: 'Ada' }, tags: ['a'] };
const { user: { name }, ...rest } = state;  // destructuring + rest
const label = `Hi ${name ?? 'guest'}`;       // template literal + nullish coalescing
const count = state.tags?.length;            // optional chaining
examples.explanation: These are the features that remove most defensive coding.

javascript.question: What is Object.assign and how does it differ from object spread?
javascript.answer: Object.assign(target, ...sources) copies own enumerable properties from the sources onto the target and returns that same mutated object. Spreading ({ ...source }) builds a new object instead. They copy the same properties - including symbol-keyed ones - so the only real difference is the target: spread cannot mutate a shared object by accident. Prefer spread in application code. Both are shallow - nested objects are still shared references.

examples.title: Mutate vs copy
examples.code:
const defaults = { retries: 3 };
const a = Object.assign({}, defaults, { retries: 5 });  // new object
const b = Object.assign(defaults, { retries: 5 });       // mutates defaults!

const c = { ...defaults, retries: 5 };                   // new object
examples.explanation: Prefer spread - Object.assign on a shared defaults object edits it for everyone.

javascript.question: How do you prevent an object from being modified?
javascript.answer: Object.freeze seals an object shallowly: existing properties cannot be reassigned or deleted, and new ones cannot be added. Nested objects are not affected, so for deep protection you freeze recursively. Object.seal allows modification but blocks adding and deleting. Reassigning an existing non-writable property throws a TypeError in strict mode and fails silently in sloppy mode. Freeze also reaches internal slots: a frozen array cannot be pushed to or sorted, because every one of those operations has to write a property on an object that is no longer extensible - that throws in both modes. What freeze never reaches is anything the object references, which is why the recursion above is the part people forget.

examples.title: Shallow vs deep freeze
examples.explanation: Freeze walks one level; nested objects must be frozen explicitly.

javascript.question: What is type coercion in JavaScript?
javascript.answer: JavaScript implicitly converts values between types when an operator or context demands it, which is why "4" - 2 is 2 but "4" + 2 is "42" - addition concatenates when either side is a string. Comparisons use abstract equality loosely: == coerces types, while === compares type and value. Coercion produces the infamous NaN whenever a string cannot be parsed as a number. Prefer explicit conversion - Number(), String(), Boolean() - and always === over ==.

examples.title: Coercion surprises
examples.code:
'4' - 2;        // 2      (numeric)
'4' + 2;        // '42'    (string concat)
'4' == 4;       // true    (loose)
'4' === 4;      // false   (strict)
3 + undefined; // NaN
examples.explanation: Arithmetic coerces to numbers, + with a string concatenates, and == coerces while === does not.

javascript.question: How do you find the minimum and maximum value in an array?
javascript.answer: Spread the array into Math.min or Math.max. Beware the argument limit: Math.min(...arr) throws a RangeError for arrays with roughly a hundred thousand elements or more, and it also fails on an empty array (Infinity for min, -Infinity for max). For large arrays reduce the values instead, and decide what an empty list should mean for your domain.

examples.title: Spread, reduce and the empty case
examples.explanation: Spread is clearest for normal data; reduce avoids the argument-count limit.

javascript.question: Why is JavaScript single-threaded, and how does the event loop keep it from blocking?
javascript.answer: Synchronous code runs one statement at a time, in order, and nothing else runs until it finishes. Asynchronous code schedules work to run later and returns immediately, so the thread stays free to keep going. JavaScript is single-threaded because it was born as a browser scripting language: one thread per tab owns the DOM, and if multiple threads mutated the document at once the UI would race and break, so the language runs on one main thread with an event loop that yields to rendering between tasks. Single-threaded means one call stack, so exactly one thing executes at a time. It avoids blocking through the event loop and its two queues: when an async API settles (network, timer, a resolved promise), the runtime does not interrupt the current code; it queues a callback and only runs it once the stack is empty. The microtask queue (promise handlers, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) is drained completely after each task; the macrotask queue (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, browser events) runs one task at a time, then the microtask queue empties again, then the browser may paint. Long synchronous work janks the page; long async work stays responsive because the stack empties between small units. Web Workers are the escape hatch for genuinely parallel compute, with the price that they have no DOM access.

examples.title: Synchronous vs asynchronous at a glance
examples.code:
console.log('A');                       // sync: runs now, in order
const x = add(1, 2);                  // sync: result available inline
console.log(x);                       // '3' immediately

setTimeout(() => console.log('C'), 0);      // scheduled macrotask
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('B')); // scheduled microtask

console.log('D');                     // sync: runs now
// output order: A, 3, D, B, C
examples.explanation: Sync code finishes inline; async callbacks run later. Even a 0ms timer is still a task, and the microtask (B) always beats it because the microtask queue drains before the next macrotask.

examples.title: Why one thread does not block: the event loop
examples.explanation: The microtask queue empties fully after each task; the macrotask queue runs one task at a time. Callbacks never interrupt running code, so the page stays interactive for async-heavy work.

javascript.question: How do you find the second highest number in an array?
javascript.answer: I would clarify first whether duplicates count, because [10, 10, 8] is either 8 or nothing depending on what they meant, and what to return for an array with fewer than two distinct values. With that settled, one pass with two variables is the answer: walk the array once, when a value beats the current highest shift the old highest down into second place, and when it does not beat the highest but beats second, update second. Guarding the second branch with 'less than highest' is what keeps a duplicate of the winner from becoming the runner-up. That is O(n) time and O(1) extra space, versus sorting first at O(n log n) and O(n) space, and the single pass also short-circuits nothing in the worst case, so the honest comparison is about clarity rather than a big win - though on a large input it is still measurably cheaper. Edge cases I would mention rather than let them find them: empty arrays, one distinct value, NaN, and unsorted input, which the one-pass version handles by construction.

examples.title: One pass, duplicates handled explicitly
examples.explanation: The n < highest test is the whole trick: without it the repeated 10 would overwrite second and you would report 10 as the answer.

javascript.question: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
javascript.answer: A shallow copy duplicates the outermost container and copies the references inside it, so the new object is independent at the top level only - spread, Object.assign and array slice all behave this way. Mutate a nested object on the copy and you have mutated the original, which is exactly the bug that produces a UI that will not re-render or a store entry that changed without an action. A deep copy duplicates the nested structure too, so nothing is shared. The standard tool is structuredClone(), which handles cycles, Dates, Maps, Sets, RegExps and typed arrays; it refuses functions, DOM nodes and class instances that are not cloneable, which is the failure people meet first. The old alternative, JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)), silently drops undefined values, Dates become strings, functions disappear, and it throws on circular references - acceptable only for data that is genuinely JSON. The practical rule in Angular is to avoid needing a deep copy at all: update immutably at every level (spread the object and the branch you touched), because signals, OnPush and NgRx all rely on reference changes meaning something.

examples.title: Shared by reference, then properly cloned
examples.explanation: Spread copies one level, so every nested reference is still the original's; structuredClone copies the whole graph, and tells you where it stops.

javascript.question: What is a Promise, and how do you work with one?
javascript.answer: A Promise is an object that represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation, and the part worth saying precisely is that it is in one of three states - pending, fulfilled or rejected - and it settles exactly once. After it has fulfilled or rejected it never changes again, which is what separates it from a callback that can fire any number of times. You create one with new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...), but in practice you consume the promises APIs hand back, either with .then/.catch/.finally or with async/await, which is cleaner syntax over the same chain - an await pauses that function, not the thread. Composition is where promises earn their place: Promise.all runs calls in parallel and rejects as soon as one fails, allSettled waits for all of them and reports each outcome, race takes the first to settle and any takes the first to succeed. The pitfalls interviewers listen for are forgetting to return a promise inside a then, which lets the chain resolve before the inner work finishes; floating promises that nobody awaits or catches, because an unhandled rejection surfaces late and somewhere else; and awaiting in a loop when the calls are independent, which turns the total time from the slowest call into the sum of them. Angular's HttpClient returns Observables rather than promises on purpose, since an Observable can emit more than once and be cancelled, and firstValueFrom or lastValueFrom convert one when a promise really is simpler.

examples.title: States, then/catch, and the same thing with async/await
examples.explanation: The promise is pending until it settles, and it settles once - the catch covers a rejection from anywhere above it in the chain. async/await changes the look of this, not the behaviour; await only pauses the function it is written in.

examples.title: Parallel beats sequential, and the combinators
examples.explanation: Promise.all is all-or-nothing and fails fast; allSettled always waits and tells you which ones failed; race takes the first settlement, which is how a timeout is built; any takes the first success.

angular.question: What is a component in Angular?
angular.answer: A component is an Angular building block that combines an HTML template, styles and a TypeScript class that holds the logic and state. Components are standalone by default in modern Angular and import the dependencies they use directly in their imports array.

examples.title: A standalone component
examples.explanation: Template, styles and class in one place; everything it needs is listed in imports.

angular.question: What is data binding in Angular?
angular.answer: Data binding connects the component class to the template. Interpolation {{ }} and property binding [property] flow from class to view, event binding (event) flows from view to class, and two-way binding [(ngModel)] or model() flows both ways.

examples.title: Interpolation
examples.code: Hello {{ user().name }}
examples.explanation: Class -> view, rendered as text (escaped).

examples.title: Property binding
examples.explanation: Sets a DOM/component property instead of an attribute.

examples.title: Event binding
examples.code: <button (click)="save()">Save</button>
examples.explanation: View -> class: the handler receives a native or $event value.

examples.title: Two-way binding
examples.code: <input [ngModel]="name()" (ngModelChange)="name.set($event)" />
examples.explanation: Expands to a property binding plus an event binding; with signals you usually write both sides explicitly.

angular.question: What is an Angular directive?
angular.answer: A directive is a class that extends HTML behaviour — structure or presentation — without an associated template. Attribute directives change an element's appearance or behaviour, while structural directives add, remove or repeat elements in the DOM - *ngIf and *ngFor are the classic ones, replaced in modern templates by the built-in @if / @for control-flow blocks. To write one: a class with a selector that matches an attribute, element or modifier, marked standalone so templates import it directly; host bindings and host listeners expose its state, and the DOM goes through ElementRef and Renderer2 rather than nativeElement.style, because Renderer2 stays platform-safe and testable. If CSS alone can express the behaviour, CSS alone should.

examples.title: Component directive
examples.code: <app-header [title]="pageTitle()" />
examples.explanation: A component is a directive with a template - it adds a new element to the DOM.

examples.title: Structural directive
examples.code: @if (isLoggedIn()) { <app-admin /> }
examples.explanation: Structural directives add or remove DOM (@if/@for/@switch are built-ins now).

examples.title: Attribute directive
examples.code: <button matButton appAutofocus>Go</button>
examples.explanation: Attribute directives change behaviour or appearance of the host element without adding markup.

examples.title: A directive you can actually write
examples.explanation: Attribute directive: it matches an attribute, adds no markup of its own, and changes the host element - the reusable version of an inline (mouseenter) handler copied into five templates.

angular.question: What is dependency injection?
angular.answer: Dependency injection is how Angular provides the services a component or class needs. Instead of a class creating its own dependencies with new, it declares what it needs - in its constructor or with inject() - and Angular's injector resolves and supplies them, which is the "no manual instantiating" part. The advantages are loose coupling (a class depends on a token, not a concrete implementation), testability (swap in a fake via the same token), a single place to control scope and lifetime (an app-wide singleton or one instance per component or route), and easier refactoring because the wiring lives in the injector rather than being scattered through constructors. Services marked providedIn: 'root' are app-wide singletons.

examples.title: Root-provided service
examples.explanation: One instance for the whole app - inject it without listing it anywhere.

examples.title: Component-provided service
examples.explanation: A new instance per component, which is how you keep state from leaking between component instances.

angular.question: What is the difference between @Input and @Output, and how do the signal APIs change it?
angular.answer: @Input lets a parent pass data down into a child, and @Output lets the child emit an event upward - together they are the two halves of component communication. In modern Angular you use the signal APIs rather than the decorators: input() / input.required() on the way in, output() on the way out, and model() when the value both flows down and can be written back up by the child. The behavioural difference is that signal inputs and outputs are reactive - a computed() can derive from them and change detection is notified when they change - whereas decorator inputs are plain properties that you read imperatively.

examples.title: Input into a child
examples.code:
id = input.required<string>();
label = input('Untitled');
examples.explanation: Parent passes data down: <app-tag [id]="tagId" />

examples.title: Output from a child
examples.code:
removed = output<string>();
// <app-tag (removed)="onRemoved($event)" />
examples.explanation: Child emits upward so the parent can react - the other half of component communication.

angular.question: A user types in a search box and the whole page feels janky. How do you isolate the cause and fix it?
angular.answer: Profile first: use Angular DevTools to spot components running many change-detection cycles and the Chrome performance tab to confirm what is slow. Common fixes: debounceTime(300) + switchMap on the search stream so every keystroke does not hit the API, move heavy computations out of templates into pipes or a computed, add trackBy, use ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush on the growing list, and wrap high-frequency handlers like scroll in runOutsideAngular(ngZone). Fix the root cause rather than sprinkling optimizations.

examples.title: Debounce + cancel + isolate
examples.explanation: Fix the cause: one request per settled term, stale responses dropped, and the list re-renders on its own dependency only.

angular.question: A sidebar filter and a dashboard list are unrelated components but must stay in sync. How do you implement this?
angular.answer: Put the shared state in a service: a signal() (or BehaviorSubject if you need an async stream) with read/computed selectors. Keep components dumb - the list reads the signal and re-renders. For parent-to-child data use @Input/@Output; for unrelated components a shared service is the standard answer, and signals today remove the subscription boilerplate the BehaviorSubject approach needed.

examples.title: Shared service with signals
examples.explanation: The sidebar writes, the list reads - no parent, no Input/Output plumbing, and derived data stays consistent.

angular.question: The user clicks 'Save' rapidly while a POST is in flight. How do you prevent duplicate requests?
angular.answer: Use exhaustMap on the click stream: it ignores new emissions while an inner request is running and only accepts the next click after completion. That matches the intent - ignore extra clicks until the request settles. switchMap would cancel the in-flight request, which is wrong for a save; debounceTime would just delay the first click.

examples.title: Ignore clicks while saving
examples.explanation: exhaustMap drops emissions while the inner request is in flight, so one click means one request - but only because the subscription is created once.

angular.question: A dashboard must show data from three APIs, but only when all three have arrived, and it must update if any of them changes later. What operator do you use and why?
angular.answer: combineLatest: it emits only once all sources have emitted at least once and keeps emitting whenever any source changes afterwards - exactly 'render once all three exist, update on any change'. forkJoin would be wrong because it emits once and completes, so later changes never re-render. If you only needed the first combined value, forkJoin would be fine.

examples.title: combineLatest vs forkJoin
examples.explanation: combineLatest fits 'render when everything is present and keep updating'; forkJoin fits 'wait for a batch of requests'.

angular.question: There is a memory leak in production - memory grows steadily as users navigate. How do you track it down?
angular.answer: Reproduce in dev with the browser heap snapshot: take two snapshots around a navigation cycle and diff them to find detached DOM nodes or lingering references. Suspect manual subscribe() calls that were never unsubscribed, timers, and addEventListener. Fix by using the async pipe or takeUntilDestroyed(), and centralizing subscriptions so cleanup is a convention, not a discipline.

examples.title: Finding and fixing the leak
examples.explanation: In the heap snapshot, detached DOM retained by a live subscription is the giveaway; takeUntilDestroyed (or the async pipe) makes cleanup automatic.

angular.question: You need a reusable form input that works both with ngModel and inside a reactive form. How do you build it?
angular.answer: Implement ControlValueAccessor on a component: writeValue populates the control, registerOnChange/registerOnTouched wire the UI to the form model, and setDisabledState handles enable/disable. You might ask why this is needed - could you not just read the ngModel value and build the payload yourself? For one screen you could, but then the component knows nothing about the form around it. Implementing CVA makes the component speak the same contract as a native input, so it works with [(ngModel)] and with [formControl]/formControlName, participates in validation and touched/dirty/pending state, responds to form.reset(), honours setDisabledState, and composes inside a parent formGroup. The emitted value is only one part of that contract; the rest is what makes it interchangeable with a real input.

examples.title: ControlValueAccessor
examples.explanation: Implementing the four methods makes the component bindable by both ngModel and formControlName. The signatures accept null because the forms API calls them with null, for example on reset.

examples.title: Using it
examples.code:
<app-rating [(ngModel)]="score" />

<form [formGroup]="form">
  <app-rating formControlName="score" />
</form>
examples.explanation: One component, both form APIs, because it speaks the CVA contract.

angular.question: A stepper form is spread across multiple components but must behave as one form. How do you keep it consistent?
angular.answer: Own a single FormGroup instance in a parent component and pass it down (@Input) or expose it from a shared service provided at the parent scope. Each step component binds its controls to the same instance via formControlName/formGroup, and the stepper reads validity from one place. A service scoped to the feature route (rather than root) avoids leaking state across navigation.

examples.title: One FormGroup, several steps
examples.explanation: The step components never own form state - they render and validate parts of the parent's instance.

examples.title: Scoped service alternative
examples.code: @Component({ providers: [CheckoutForm] })   // one instance per checkout flow
examples.explanation: Providing the form on the parent (or a route-scoped service) avoids stale state surviving navigation.

angular.question: How do you implement role-based access control - restricting routes by role and hiding UI elements?
angular.answer: Two layers: a route guard canActivateFn checks whether the logged-in role may enter a route (and redirects otherwise), while a structural directive (like *appHasRole) conditionally renders UI for a role. Keep the user's roles in a shared service/signal read by both. Never rely on hiding UI alone - guards must also enforce the route, and the server must enforce authorization anyway.

examples.title: Route guard + structural directive
examples.explanation: The guard protects the route and (with canMatch) the download; the directive only shapes the UI. The backend must still authorise.

angular.question: Two routes must be lazy-loaded, but only admin users may reach the Reports route. How do you set that up?
angular.answer: Use a guard that checks the user's role from the auth store before entry. Prefer canMatch (which runs before the module is loaded) over canActivate only, so the lazy Reports bundle is never downloaded for unauthorized users. Pair it with loadComponent routing so admin access and code-splitting both hold.

examples.title: canMatch keeps the bundle private
examples.explanation: canActivate checks after the route is matched (chunk already requested); canMatch blocks earlier, so unauthorised users never download the code.

angular.question: What is the difference between the constructor and ngOnInit?
angular.answer: The constructor runs when the component instance is created, before inputs are resolved - Angular best practice is to use it only for dependency injection and minimal setup. ngOnInit runs after the first ngOnChanges, once the component's inputs are set, so it is the right place to read input values and kick off initialization logic or long-lived subscriptions.

examples.title: Constructor vs ngOnInit
examples.explanation: DI only in constructor; initialization that reads inputs in ngOnInit.

angular.question: What is the async pipe and how does it prevent memory leaks?
angular.answer: The async pipe subscribes to an Observable in the template ({{ users$ | async }}) and unsubscribes automatically when the component is destroyed. That removes the need for a manual subscription and the classic leak where a component subscribes in ngOnInit but never unsubscribes in ngOnDestroy. It pairs naturally with OnPush change detection.

examples.code:
@for (u of users$ | async; track u.id) {
  • {{ u.name }}
    • }
examples.explanation: async pipe auto-unsubscribes when component is destroyed.

angular.question: What are route guards and which ones do you know?
angular.answer: Route guards decide whether navigation proceeds. canActivate/canActivateFn checks a route's entry once matched, canMatch blocks the route from even being considered (running before module load - best for lazy security), and canDeactivate asks before leaving a dirty form. They are functions or services returning boolean, an observable/promise, or a redirect URL tree.

examples.title: Route guards
examples.explanation: canActivateFn/canMatch gate navigation/loads.

angular.question: What is an HTTP interceptor and what are typical use cases?
angular.answer: An interceptor sits in the request/response pipeline and lets you transform a request or observe a response centrally, instead of repeating logic per call. Common uses: attaching an auth token header, global error handling and retries, logging, and loading indicators. In modern Angular it is implemented as a function returning next.handle(req) in the chain.

examples.title: HTTP interceptor (function form)
examples.explanation: Modern functional interceptor: clone and chain with next.

angular.question: What is a pipe and the difference between pure and impure pipes?
angular.answer: A pipe transforms a value in the template ({{ value | date: 'short' }}). A pure pipe (the default) runs its transform only when Angular detects a "pure change" to an input argument: a change to a primitive value (string, number, boolean) or a new object/array reference. That is why mutating data in place - pushing into an array or editing a property of an object - does not re-run a pure pipe: the reference is unchanged, so Angular sees no change. That is the classic pure-pipe pitfall. An impure pipe (pure: false) runs during every change detection cycle - every keystroke, click or timer tick - so it does pick up mutations and data changing independently of its arguments, but at a real performance cost. Make pure the rule and impure the exception.

examples.title: Why a pure pipe misses a mutation
examples.code:
items.push(newItem);         // same array reference -> a pure pipe does not re-run
this.items.set([...items]);  // new reference -> the pipe re-runs
examples.explanation: A pure pipe keys off the argument's reference, so an in-place mutation is invisible to it; hand it a new array (or use an impure pipe).

examples.title: Pure vs impure pipe
examples.explanation: pure (default) runs on primitive or reference changes only; impure runs every change detection cycle.

angular.question: What is content projection (ng-content)?
angular.answer: Content projection lets a parent component pass markup into a child's template via <ng-content>. In a card or modal component the child defines named slots with <ng-content select="[slot='header']"> and the parent fills them by putting slot="header" on its content, which makes the component reusable without prop-drilling markup. Multi-slot projection uses the select attribute; a catch-all ng-content without select grabs everything else.

examples.explanation: select targets named slots; unnamed ng-content is the default.

angular.question: A username field must show "already taken" while the user types, using a backend check. How do you implement it?
angular.answer: Reach for an AsyncValidator, not a manual subscribe. Angular runs async validators through the same FormControl status pipeline as sync validators, so the control goes PENDING while the check is in flight and then VALID or INVALID - and you wire the disabled state yourself from form.pending, Angular will not do that for you. Two rules matter. Debounce before hitting the network, with a timer inside the validator. And skip re-checking an unchanged value - but note that distinctUntilChanged() belongs on the valueChanges stream that drives the check, not inside the validator, because Angular re-runs the validator as a fresh subscription on every value change and there is no previous emission for it to compare against. Always catchError inside the validator and return null - a network failure is not the user's fault, so it must not mark the field invalid and block submit.

examples.title: Async validator factory (debounced + failure-tolerant)
examples.explanation: The factory takes the service as an argument because inject() is not available inside the function the validator returns. Dedupe the value upstream on valueChanges with distinctUntilChanged() - each validator run is a fresh subscription, so it has nothing to compare against.

examples.title: Wiring it up and showing the three states
examples.explanation: pending covers the in-flight window, invalid covers a real backend rejection, and the submit button stays disabled while either is true - that last part is your binding, not Angular's behaviour.

angular.question: A component loads its data in ngOnInit from a service. How do you test that the data actually renders?
angular.answer: Configure the test with a fake for the dependency, not the real HTTP stack. Provide a spy object with TestBed, assert the component called it, then trigger change detection and assert on the rendered DOM. Use signals plus whenStable rather than relying on a timer, so the test is deterministic. Signal inputs must be set through componentRef.setInput, because assigning to the input field directly bypasses the signal. Also test the failure path - the empty and error states are where component bugs hide.

examples.title: Test with a spy for the service
examples.explanation: No HTTP, no async pipe waiting games - the fake returns a synchronous observable.

examples.title: Signal inputs and the error path
examples.explanation: Asserting the empty/error state catches the bugs that only appear in production.

angular.question: Forms must be generated at runtime from a JSON schema sent by the backend. How do you build them?
angular.answer: Build the FormGroup imperatively from the schema and drive the template from the same schema, so adding a field needs no component change. Walk the schema, addControl per field, attach validators from declarative hints (required, minLength, email), and use nonNullable controls for inputs so you get strings and numbers instead of null unions. For nested objects recurse into child FormGroups; for anything with conditional visibility or cross-field rules, hand off to a library such as Formly or Angular's signal forms instead of reinventing the DSL. Always cache the generated group when the schema is static, otherwise you recreate controls on every detection cycle.

examples.explanation: Validators come from data, so the schema is the single source of truth for validation.

examples.code:
<form [formGroup]="form">
  @for (f of schema; track f.name) {
    <label [for]="f.name">{{ f.label }}</label>
    <input [id]="f.name" [formControlName]="f.name" />
    @if (form.controls[f.name].hasError('required')) {
      <small>{{ f.label }} is required</small>
    }
  }
  <button [disabled]="form.invalid">Save</button>
</form>
examples.explanation: The template never names a specific field, so backend schema changes ship without code.

angular.question: How would you structure a multi-role enterprise Angular app so it stays maintainable as features keep being added?
angular.answer: Use three layers with a strict dependency direction: core holds singletons and app-wide wiring (interceptors, guards, app config, root services), shared holds reusable presentation (UI components, pipes, directives) that depend only on core, and features holds the domain code - one folder per role or bounded context, each with its own components, routes and models. Lazy-load each feature and gate it with a role guard. The rule that keeps it from rotting is that features must not import from other features; when two features need the same thing it moves to shared or into a small publishable library. Prefer explicit imports over barrel files, because barrels pull unrelated code into every chunk and blur the dependency graph.

examples.title: Folder structure
examples.code:
src/app/
  core/            # providedIn:'root' services, interceptors, guards, app.config
    auth/
    http/
  shared/          # reusable UI - imports core only
    ui/            # button, dialog, data-table
    pipes/
  features/        # domain code - never imported across
    admin/         # routes.ts + components + models
    manager/
    reports/
  app.routes.ts    # top-level lazy routes only

libs/
  ui-kit/          # publishable lib when shared grows
examples.explanation: core and shared stay small and stable; features absorb all the churn.

examples.code:
