  { path: 'admin', canMatch: [roleGuard('admin')],
    loadChildren: () => import('./features/admin/routes').then(m => m.ADMIN_ROUTES) },
  { path: 'manager', canMatch: [roleGuard('manager')],
    loadChildren: () => import('./features/manager/routes').then(m => m.MANAGER_ROUTES) },
  { path: 'reports', canMatch: [roleGuard('admin')],
    loadComponent: () => import('./features/reports/report-list').then(c => c.ReportList) },
];
examples.explanation: canMatch keeps the chunk from even being fetched by users who cannot use it.

angular.question: A third-party chat widget needs its <script> injected and global config loaded. How do you integrate it without breaking SSR or encapsulation?
angular.answer: Wrap it in a service plus a thin component or directive rather than scattering script tags. Create the service with Renderer2 so the script node is added and later removed through Angular, and only in the browser - guard with isPlatformBrowser or run the work in afterNextRender, which never executes on the server. Load the configuration with provideAppInitializer so the app blocks until the config exists, instead of racing it during bootstrap. If the vendor injects its own styles into document.head, isolate it in a wrapper component with ViewEncapsulation.None; if it needs a framework, add it as an external script in angular.json rather than injecting at runtime. Always keep the cleanup handle - chat widgets keep global listeners.

examples.title: SSR-safe loader with Renderer2
examples.explanation: On the server this is a no-op, and the DOM node is created and removed through Angular.

examples.title: Blocking bootstrap on config
examples.explanation: provideAppInitializer replaces the deprecated APP_INITIALIZER token; Encapsulation.None keeps the vendor's global styles working.

angular.question: You need to move an application from an older Angular major to a current one. How do you plan the upgrade?
angular.answer: Upgrade one major at a time with ng update, and never jump two majors in one branch - the migrations assume the previous layout. Before running anything, read the update guide for that version: it lists breaking changes, the required Node and TypeScript and RxJS versions, and flags removed APIs. Then move in this order: Angular packages, then third-party libraries whose majors are coupled to it (Angular Material must match), then tooling and CI images. Let ng update rewrite angular.json, tsconfig and the entry files for you instead of editing them by hand. Afterwards check the bundle budgets, remove obsolete polyfills, rebuild, and fix whatever the compiler flags - deprecations usually surface as compile errors once the old name is removed. Verify on a branch with tests and manual smoke checks before merging.

examples.code:
# pre-flight: node -v, then branch + tests green
ng update @angular/cli@17 @angular/core@17 @angular/material@17
npm run build            # read every warning before continuing

ng update @angular/cli@18 @angular/core@18 @angular/material@18
npm run build

ng update @angular/cli@19 @angular/core@19 @angular/material@19
npm run build && npm test
examples.explanation: Material and other libs must move in lockstep, or you get injection-token and template type errors that are hard to read.

examples.explanation: Budgets turn a silent bundle regression into a build failure, and stale polyfills are dead weight.

angular.question: Two separately deployed Angular apps must share one login. How do you implement shared authentication?
angular.answer: Give ownership of the session to one place and treat the other app as a client of it. Preferred design: a shell or BFF owns an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, and each app verifies the session with a cheap GET /me during provideAppInitializer before it bootstraps - so a user with an expired session lands on login instead of rendering a broken shell. Put that logic in a shared library so both apps run identical code. Never store access tokens in localStorage if you can avoid it: anything in localStorage is readable by injected script, so use the cookie plus CSRF protection, and keep any token in memory only. To keep the two apps in sync, broadcast login and logout over BroadcastChannel when they share an origin (cookies ignore the port, so :4300 sees the cookie set by :4200); across origins you need a real shared backend session or an iframe/postMessage broker.

examples.title: Shell owns the cookie, apps verify
examples.explanation: Session verification before bootstrap means both apps agree on auth state from the first render.

examples.title: Sync logout between apps on the same origin
examples.explanation: Cookies are shared across ports on one domain, so the logout must hit the server - clearing client state alone leaves the cookie valid.

examples.title: Memory-only token in an interceptor
examples.explanation: An XSS bug cannot read the token out of storage; it can only use it while the page lives.

angular.question: Production errors are vague and hard to trace. What do you set up for monitoring?
angular.answer: Put three layers in place. First, an error tracker (Sentry or similar) with its official Angular integration, which reports uncaught errors and rejections, attaches release and environment tags, and - critically - uploads source maps so the production stack traces are readable. Second, a global ErrorHandler that forwards anything Angular catches to the tracker with user context and scrubs tokens and PII before sending. Third, an HTTP interceptor that normalises every failure into one shape, attaches a correlation id that also goes into your backend logs, and rethrows so callers still handle their own errors. Add breadcrumbs for the user actions leading up to the failure, then alert on thresholds rather than on every error, or the channel gets ignored.

examples.title: Global ErrorHandler that scrubs
examples.explanation: One place decides what leaves the browser, so no component accidentally leaks PII.

examples.title: Normalising HTTP errors with a correlation id
examples.explanation: One error type for the whole app, plus an id that ties the browser report to the server log.

examples.title: Readable production stacks
examples.explanation: Hidden source maps are uploaded to the tracker and excluded from the bundle you deploy.

angular.question: What are micro-frontends, and how would you implement them in Angular?
angular.answer: A micro-frontend splits one UI into independently built, independently deployed applications owned by separate teams, stitched together into a single product for the user. In Angular the common approaches are: module federation (Webpack 5, or Native Federation for the esbuild/Vite application builder), where a shell loads remote apps at runtime and shares framework singletons; Web Components via Angular Elements, where each micro-app is exported as a custom element and may even be written in another framework; and iframes for hard isolation at the cost of integration and performance. The genuinely hard parts are not the loading mechanism. Angular must be a shared singleton, not one copy per remote. Routing from the shell into a remote has to be designed. The apps need an agreed way to communicate (custom events, a shared event bus, or a shared state library). And a shared design system has to stop the UI drifting. Add the operational cost too: several pipelines, several versions of shared dependencies, and a much harder end-to-end testing story. The honest framing is that a modular monolith in an Nx workspace is the better default, and micro-frontends are justified only when independent deployment and team autonomy outweigh that complexity.

examples.title: Runtime composition with Native Federation
examples.explanation: The shell is a normal Angular app; the remote is a separately deployed one loaded lazily at runtime. Shared packages (including @angular/core) are configured as singletons so there is one framework instance.

examples.title: A framework-agnostic boundary with Angular Elements
examples.explanation: Exposing the app as a custom element gives a clean boundary that a legacy host page, or a host built with another framework, can consume.

angular.question: How do you write a custom validator and an async validator in Angular reactive forms?
angular.answer: A validator is just a function that takes a control and returns either null (valid) or an errors object. For a reusable one, return a factory so you can pass a parameter: forbiddenName('admin') returns (control: AbstractControl) => ValidationErrors | null. Attach it when you build the FormControl, or later with addValidators(). The keys of the returned object are what the template switches on, so expose the key and the value that failed rather than baking a message into the validator. Cross-field rules such as password === confirmPassword belong on the parent FormGroup, not the control, because one control cannot see its sibling. An async validator is the same idea but returns an Observable or a Promise; the control goes to status 'pending' while it runs, and Angular only runs it once the synchronous validators pass. Always debounce it and cancel stale work (or use updateOn: 'blur'), otherwise you fire a server request on every keystroke and race the responses. In template-driven forms the same logic is packaged as a directive registered on NG_VALIDATORS / NG_ASYNC_VALIDATORS; in reactive forms the function is enough.

examples.title: A reusable synchronous validator
examples.explanation: Return null when valid and a keyed errors object when not; the template reacts to form.controls.name.hasError('forbiddenName').

examples.title: Cross-field rule and an async availability check
examples.explanation: One control cannot see its sibling, so the group validator compares them; timer() plus switchMap debounces and cancels stale checks so an older response cannot overwrite a newer one.

angular.question: How does JWT authentication work in the UI, what is sent to the backend, and what does the backend do with it?
angular.answer: The UI posts credentials (username and password) once; the backend checks them and returns a signed token, usually with a short expiry, plus often a longer-lived refresh token. A JWT is three base64url parts: header.payload.signature. Where you store it matters. The safest option is an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie that the server sets, because JavaScript and therefore an XSS attack cannot read it; if you keep it in JavaScript, prefer memory for the access token and treat localStorage as XSS-exposed. The important division of responsibility is that the UI never verifies the signature and never trusts claims for security. It may decode the payload to read exp or a display name, but that is cosmetic only: decoding is not verifying. On every call the client sends the token, typically Authorization: Bearer <token> (with withCredentials: true when it lives in a cookie). The backend verifies the signature with the secret or public key, checks exp/nbf, issuer and audience, then reads the claims (sub, roles) to authorise the request. In Angular an HTTP interceptor attaches the header and handles a 401 by refreshing the token and retrying once. A token is a credential, so never log it or put it in a URL. One more line interviewers listen for: route guards and role-hidden buttons are user experience, not enforcement - they stop an honest user, not anyone with curl - so the backend authorises every protected call again, and the UI renders a 403 from the API as a state to handle rather than a path that cannot happen.

examples.title: Attach the token and refresh on 401
examples.explanation: One place adds the header to every request; a 401 triggers a refresh and a single retry instead of an error surfacing on every in-flight call.

examples.title: The UI only decodes; the backend verifies
examples.explanation: Decoding is not verifying: the payload is attacker-visible and attacker-editable, so it is fine for display and useless for a security decision.

angular.question: What are pipes in Angular, and how do you create a custom pipe?
angular.answer: A pipe transforms a value for display, written in a template with the | operator, so the component keeps the raw data while the view shows a formatted version. Angular ships DatePipe, CurrencyPipe, DecimalPipe, PercentPipe, UpperCasePipe, TitleCasePipe, SlicePipe, JsonPipe, KeyValuePipe and AsyncPipe. A custom pipe is a small class decorated with @Pipe({ name: 'truncate' }) that implements PipeTransform with a transform(value, ...args) method; you then add the class to the standalone component's imports (or declare it in a shared module) and use it as {{ text | truncate: 20 }}. Pipes are pure by default: Angular re-runs one only when its input reference changes, so the transform must be deterministic and free of side effects. Setting pure: false re-runs it on every change detection cycle, which is why an impure pipe over a large list is a well-known performance trap. Keep pipes for display-only transformations; heavy work belongs in computed() or a component, and async state belongs to the async pipe.

examples.explanation: Extra arguments after the first are passed with colons; the pipe is reusable because it is a standalone class, and correct because a string input is compared by value.

examples.title: Pure vs impure in practice
examples.explanation: Pure pipes trade freshness for speed; if a mutation must be reflected, either produce a new reference or derive the value from a computed() signal instead.

angular.question: What is new in the recent Angular releases?
angular.answer: The last few majors have been mostly about signals, zoneless and the build. v17 introduced the built-in control flow (@if/@for/@switch), @defer for lazy-loading template chunks, and the new esbuild/Vite application builder that replaced webpack. v18 brought experimental zoneless change detection and the @let template variable. v19 made standalone the default (standalone: true was no longer needed), shipped incremental hydration, and added the resource() API for async state. v20 stabilised effect, linkedSignal and toSignal, made incremental hydration and route-level render modes stable, promoted zoneless to developer preview, and introduced the experimental httpResource. v21 made zoneless the default for new apps and stopped including zone.js by default, released experimental Signal Forms, made Vitest the default test runner, provided HttpClient by default, and launched Angular Aria in developer preview. v22 stabilised Signal Forms, Angular Aria and the async reactivity APIs (resource/httpResource), made OnPush the default change detection strategy for new apps, and renamed ChangeDetectionStrategy.Default to Eager. The theme across all of it is signal-first, zoneless and performance by default, and every claim here is worth checking against the release blog, because the pace is fast.

examples.title: New control flow and defer
examples.explanation: Built-in control flow replaced the structural directives; @defer splits a component into its own bundle and loads it only when its trigger fires.

examples.title: Signals and zoneless by default
examples.explanation: New Angular apps are zoneless and use OnPush by default, so change detection is driven by signal writes and inputs instead of zone.js patching every browser event.

angular.question: How does change detection work in Angular with zone.js, and how does it work now without it? Walk through what happens from root to child when an event fires in a child.
angular.answer: Change detection is Angular asking 'did anything I rendered need to update?', and the mechanism differs by era. With zone.js: zone patches browser APIs (addEventListener, setTimeout, promises, XHR), and when any async task settles it notifies Angular, which runs change detection from the root component down to every leaf. Under the default strategy every component in the tree is visited and its template bindings compared by reference, re-rendering subtrees with new values. So an event in a deeply nested child still triggers a full root-to-leaf pass, because zone only knows that something async happened, not where. In the zoneless era (the default since Angular 21) the framework does not patch globals. It tracks precise triggers - a signal a template reads being written, an input changing, a host or template listener firing, markForCheck(), or an attached view - and a scheduler runs change detection for exactly those components and their descendants, with OnPush as the default. The traversal is still top-down from root to child, but only inside the subtree that actually changed; untouched branches are skipped entirely. The mental model: with zones it is 'check everything after any asynchronous work'; zoneless it is 'check the minimum subtree that something actually touched'.

examples.title: With zone.js: patch, then walk the whole tree
examples.explanation: Zone's granularity is 'some async task settled', not 'this component changed', so the default is a full-tree pass; OnPush is how you opt subtrees out of it.

examples.title: Zoneless: the signal knows where it changed
examples.explanation: The signal carries dependency information, so change detection is notification-based: unaffected branches are never visited, and the root-to-child traversal happens only inside the subtree that changed.

angular.question: What are the advantages of using Renderer2 instead of touching the DOM directly?
angular.answer: Renderer2 is Angular's abstraction layer over the DOM, injected per component, and its advantages are about portability, lifecycle and safety rather than speed. First, platform safety: it creates elements through Angular's abstraction, so the same code runs in the browser, during server-side rendering (where document does not exist) and in Web Workers, instead of crashing on a direct document.createElement call. Second, it plays by Angular's rules: elements it creates are tied into component style encapsulation and are cleaned up when the component is destroyed. Third, lifecycle: Renderer2.listening() returns a teardown function and Angular invokes destroy() at component teardown, so listeners and elements you add imperatively do not leak. Fourth, it is a deliberate, audited API: manipulating the DOM through the renderer keeps you out of raw innerHTML and is the documented path for anything a template cannot express. The honest limit: Renderer2 is not a reactivity tool - DOM changes it makes are not reflected in state, so in the zoneless/signal default you still own keeping the template and the DOM in agreement. And not everything needs it: structural work belongs in templates, and for plain element access Angular also exposes the DOCUMENT token.

examples.title: SSR-safe imperative DOM work
examples.explanation: Read through ElementRef, write through Renderer2: addClass and listen keep working during SSR and are torn down with the directive, where raw window/document would crash the server render.

examples.title: Listening returns a teardown
examples.explanation: Renderer2 tracks what you attached and disposes it on destroy, so imperative DOM code cannot leave orphan listeners behind.

angular.question: What is view encapsulation in Angular, and what are its types?
angular.answer: View encapsulation controls how far the CSS you write in a component's styles reaches. Emulated (the default) rewrites your styles during compilation: every element of the component gets a unique attribute such as _ngcontent-abc123, and every selector gets the same attribute appended, so the rules only match that component. You get the isolation of shadow DOM without actually using it; the trade-off is rewritten CSS at build time and the fact that it is not impenetrable - :host, :host-context and ::ng-deep still reach across it. ShadowDom puts the component's template into a real shadow root, so its styles are fully isolated from the document: nothing leaks in and nothing leaks out; the price is that global styles and external libraries stop affecting the component. None adds no scoping at all: the component's styles become global document styles. Choose Emulated for normal component styling, None when you deliberately want global CSS (often for a styles file at app level), and ShadowDom for a strict public widget where hard isolation matters more than inheriting the app's theme.

examples.title: Emulated: attribute rewriting
examples.explanation: The attribute on both selector and element keeps the rule inside the component while the DOM stays in the normal document - that is what makes it the cheap default.

examples.title: ShadowDom vs None at a glance
examples.code:
ViewEncapsulation.ShadowDom
  - template goes inside a real shadow root
  - styles fully isolated: nothing leaks in or out
  - global styles and third-party libs stop applying
  - use for a strict standalone widget

ViewEncapsulation.None
  - no scoping at all: styles are injected globally
  - component's CSS can affect anything (name collisions!)
  - use only when you deliberately want document-level CSS
examples.explanation: The two ends of the spectrum: hard isolation for a public widget, no isolation when you opt out on purpose; Emulated sits between them as the day-to-day default.

angular.question: What are the Angular component lifecycle hooks, and how do they change in the signal-based era?
angular.answer: Lifecycle hooks are the calls Angular makes as a component is created, updated and torn down. Creation order: constructor (plain TypeScript, nothing bound yet), ngOnChanges (runs before ngOnInit and again on every decorated @Input change, handing you a SimpleChanges object of previous/current values), ngOnInit (once, after inputs resolve), ngDoCheck (every change detection pass, for custom checks), ngAfterContentInit and ngAfterContentChecked (projected content), ngAfterViewInit and ngAfterViewChecked (the component's own view), then ngOnDestroy (teardown, where manual subscriptions, listeners and timers must be unwound). The list is unchanged in the signal era; what changes is what you reach for. Signal inputs do not fire ngOnChanges - it is decorated-input only - so previous/current logic moves to an effect() that tracks the input. constructor becomes the natural place to set up signals, because input() signals are readable immediately and need no waiting pass. ngDoCheck and the ...Checked hooks exist for pain cases that rarely arise now, since a signal a template reads schedules exactly the update it needs. computed() replaces most derived-value bookkeeping, and the cleanup that used to live in ngOnDestroy is handled by DestroyRef and by effect() and afterRenderEffect() that dispose themselves with the component. So a modern component leans on computed/effect plus OnInit and OnDestroy, and the rest of the pipeline is mostly invisible.

examples.title: The lifecycle in order
examples.code:
constructor()            // plain TS; inputs not resolved yet
ngOnChanges()            // every @Input change, incl. the first
ngOnInit()               // once: component ready
ngDoCheck()              // every change detection pass
ngAfterContentInit()     // projected content ready
ngAfterContentChecked()
ngAfterViewInit()        // own view ready
ngAfterViewChecked()
ngOnDestroy()            // teardown: unsubscribe, clear timers
examples.explanation: The full pipeline runs creation -> change -> destruction; the only two you will consciously use most days are constructor/onInit and onDestroy.

examples.explanation: Signal inputs bypass ngOnChanges by design, so tracked changes move to effect() and derived values move to computed(); that is the main way hooks shrink in the signal era.

angular.question: What are the Angular route guards, with a small example of each?
angular.answer: Route guards are functions the router runs while resolving a navigation to decide whether it proceeds. The current API is functional: canActivate (may this route be entered - auth/access control), canActivateChild (same check for every child of a route, protecting a whole section), canMatch (participates in route matching, picking between several route objects for the same URL - feature flag or user type), canDeactivate (may we leave - unsaved changes), and resolve (prefetch data before the component renders; generally discouraged today, prefer loading after navigation with a loading state). Each guard returns boolean, a UrlTree to redirect, or an Observable/Promise of those. You can list several guards on a route; they run in order and the first false or UrlTree stops navigation. The old class-based guards (CanActivate, CanActivateChild, CanDeactivate, Resolve - and CanLoad, removed in v15) still appear in legacy code; functional guards run inside the injection context, so inject() works directly and testing one is just calling a function. Two things separate a senior answer from a list: guards are not a security boundary - they shape what the UI lets you do, while the server authorises every request regardless - and each piece owns one job. Guards decide whether navigation proceeds, resolvers (used sparingly, because they delay navigation) prepare data before activation, HTTP services own the calls, and interceptors own what is cross-cutting about them, such as the auth header and a standard error shape.

examples.title: canActivate, canMatch and canDeactivate
examples.explanation: Return false to block navigation, a UrlTree to redirect; guards run in listed order, and inject() works inside them because they execute in the injection context.

examples.title: canActivateChild protects a whole section
examples.explanation: One guard covers every child, so a newly added admin sub-page cannot be forgotten; a UrlTree gracefully redirects instead of failing the navigation.

angular.question: How do you embed an iframe such as a YouTube video in Angular, and what are DomSanitizer, SafeResourceUrl and bypassSecurityTrustResourceUrl?
angular.answer: Angular treats anything that can execute code as untrusted by default. That includes an iframe's src, an img src, a javascript: link and [innerHTML]: these bindings are sanitized, and anything Angular cannot prove safe is stripped or blocked before it reaches the DOM. DomSanitizer is the injectable that sits at that boundary - it is how you tell Angular a value is safe - and its methods map to the exact context the value will be used in. For an iframe the context is RESOURCE_URL, so the correct call is bypassSecurityTrustResourceUrl(url), which returns a SafeResourceUrl: a wrapper type, not a string, that marks the value as trusted for that binding and stops the sanitizer from touching it. That is the whole reason SafeResourceUrl exists - it is Angular's ticket saying 'I vouch for this resource URL'. What keeps it safe is the rule that you only bypass when you control or strictly validate the input. The safe pattern is to never echo raw data into the src: parse a video id from an allow-list of hosts and rebuild the URL from that id, so a hostile string can never reach the iframe. Bypassing with an unvalidated user-supplied URL is how XSS sneaks in, because a crafted src can point at attacker content that runs under your origin. Finally, trust is per-value: the wrapper applies only to the binding you bind it to, and the same string used anywhere else is still sanitized.

examples.title: Embed only after validating the input
examples.explanation: The id is matched against a fixed pattern and the URL is assembled from that id only, so the value you mark trusted is something you constructed - an attacker cannot smuggle arbitrary content into the src.

examples.title: The trust contexts at a glance
examples.explanation: Pick the bypass that matches the binding: iframe/video sources need the ResourceUrl flavour, not TrustUrl. The wrapper is per-value, so using it does not weaken sanitization anywhere else.

angular.question: What does ViewportScroller do, and when would you reach for it?
angular.answer: ViewportScroller is Angular's small abstraction over "scroll the page". It gives you getScrollPosition(), scrollToPosition([x, y]), scrollToAnchor(id), setOffset(margin) and setHistoryScrollRestoration() without touching window or document yourself, which matters because the router drives those same methods and because a test can swap in a fake instead of scrolling jsdom. The default implementation is BrowserViewportScroller - window.scrollTo and history.scrollRestoration under the hood. You reach for it directly in two situations. First, a component that is reused across navigations: when only a route parameter changes, Angular does not recreate the component and the router has no reason to scroll, so the new content opens at the old offset. Reading the parameter inside an afterRenderEffect and calling scrollToPosition([0, 0]) fixes it, and the afterRender principle is that the DOM has to be laid out before you write to its scroll. Second, anchor and offset cases - scrollToAnchor() for a fragment, setOffset() so a sticky header does not cover the target. What you normally should not do is hand-roll scrolling for route changes at all: provideRouter(routes, withInMemoryScrolling({ scrollPositionRestoration: 'enabled', anchorScrolling: 'enabled' })) installs RouterScroller, which listens to navigation events and calls ViewportScroller for you. Use the service directly only for in-place changes the router cannot see, like a reused parameterised component.

examples.title: Reset the scroll when only the route parameter changes
examples.explanation: When only the parameter changes, Angular reuses the component and the router does not scroll, so the next question would otherwise open at the previous scroll offset. The signal read is what registers the dependency; the afterRender effect is what stops the scroll being clamped against the old, shorter view.

examples.title: Let the router do it app-wide
examples.explanation: withInMemoryScrolling installs RouterScroller, which subscribes to router events and scrolls through ViewportScroller for you - restoration on history navigation, top on a fresh navigation, and fragments via scrollToAnchor. Reach for the service directly only for changes the router cannot detect, such as a reused parameterised component.

angular.question: What is the NgRx SignalStore, and which features do you compose to build one?
angular.answer: SignalStore is NgRx's signal-native state container, shipped in @ngrx/signals. You declare a store by calling signalStore(...) with an optional config followed by a sequence of features; it returns an injectable service that you register with { providedIn: 'root' } for global state, or in a providers array for component/route-scoped state where it is disposed with that injector. State is added with withState(initialState) - the type must be a record/object literal - and every slice becomes a signal on the store, with nested properties exposed lazily as DeepSignals such as store.filter.query(). Derived values are declared with withComputed(({ books, filter }) => ({ booksCount: computed(() => books().length) })); its factory runs in an injection context and any plain function it returns is wrapped in computed() for you. Behaviour lives in withMethods((store, service = inject(Service)) => ({ ... })), and state is written only through patchState(store, patch) or patchState(store, (state) => patch), which shallow-merges the patch and keeps updates immutable. withHooks({ onInit, onDestroy }) adds store-level lifecycle logic, withProps adds static values, observables or injected dependencies, signalStoreFeature builds reusable custom features, and withEntities manages collections. State is protected by default - calling patchState on the store from outside one of its methods throws unless you opt out with { protectedState: false } - which keeps every change flowing through the store's own methods. For async work you either write a plain async method or reach for rxMethod from @ngrx/signals/rxjs-interop, which turns an RxJS pipeline into a method you call with a signal, a value or an observable. SignalStore is the recommended choice for feature and local state, while @ngrx/store remains the tool for large global state.

examples.title: State, computed signals and methods in one store
examples.explanation: Each withState slice becomes a signal (filter and its nested query() too); withComputed derives read-only signals; withMethods is the only place patchState is called, so state changes through named, testable operations.

examples.title: Reactive async work with rxMethod
examples.explanation: rxMethod wraps an RxJS pipeline in a store method; hand it a signal, a value or an observable and each emission is debounced and switched, while tapResponse keeps the loading and error state in sync.

angular.question: How does the NgRx Store work - actions, reducers, selectors and effects?
angular.answer: @ngrx/store is RxJS-powered global state management inspired by Redux, built around a single immutable state tree held by the Store service. Store is both an observer of state, via store.select(selector), and an observer of actions, via store.dispatch(action). There are four moving parts. Actions are plain objects that describe unique events; createAction('[Source] Event') creates one and props<{...}>() attaches a typed payload. Reducers are pure, synchronous functions that take the current state and the latest action and return a new state - never a mutation - using createReducer(initialState, on(action, handler)) (or a switch statement in older code); every registered reducer receives every action, and each on() decides whether it cares. Selectors are pure, memoized functions that select, derive and compose slices: createFeatureSelector<T>('key') reads a feature slice and createSelector(...) composes it into a read model, returning the cached value while its inputs are unchanged. Effects are injectable RxJS streams (createEffect + ofType) that listen for actions and perform side effects such as HTTP or storage, then dispatch new actions on success or failure - reducers must stay pure, so impure work belongs here, not in a reducer. The flow is strictly one-directional: a component dispatches an action, reducers compute the next state, selectors emit the new slice to subscribers, and effects react to the same action stream and dispatch follow-up actions. When an action is dispatched it is always processed by the reducers first and then by the effects. State is registered with provideStore(reducers) and provideState('feature', reducer) in standalone apps, or StoreModule.forRoot / StoreModule.forFeature in NgModules, together with provideEffects / EffectsModule; because updates are immutable, a new reference signals change, which pairs well with OnPush and memoized selectors. In CQRS terms the reducers are the write model and the selectors the read model. For local or component state, prefer NgRx SignalStore and keep the global Store for app-wide state.

examples.title: Actions and a reducer
examples.explanation: createAction names each event and props() types its payload; createReducer pairs the initial state with on() handlers that return a new state via the spread operator, so the previous reference is never mutated.

examples.title: Effects run the side effects
examples.explanation: An effect filters the action stream with ofType, performs the HTTP call, and maps the result back to success or failure actions; the reducers stay pure because the impure work lives here.

examples.title: Selectors feed the component; it only dispatches
examples.explanation: createFeatureSelector reads the 'books' slice and createSelector composes memoized read models. Register the slice with provideStore({ books: booksReducer }) and the effect with provideEffects(BooksEffects); the component then only dispatches actions and selects slices, never touching the state object.

angular.question: How do you make an Angular application accessible?
angular.answer: Accessibility is mostly HTML discipline, then focus management, then testing. Start with real elements: button, a, label, fieldset, nav, main and heading levels give you keyboard behaviour, roles and announced names for free, whereas a div with a click handler gives you none of it. Associate every control with a label, keep a logical heading order, and give images and icon-only controls an accessible name. Keyboard is the floor: everything reachable, visible focus, no traps, and focus moved deliberately when a dialog opens or a route changes. Then the dynamic parts - announce results and validation through aria-live or role=status, and use ARIA only where native semantics cannot express it, because a wrong attribute is worse than none. Angular's CDK gives me focus trapping and overlays, and Material components ship with the semantics built in, but they cannot invent the labels or the structure; that stays my job. In practice I target WCAG 2.2 AA, run axe and the angular-eslint accessibility rules in CI so regressions fail the build, and finish with a manual pass - keyboard first, then a screen reader on the main journeys - because automation catches maybe a third of the real problems.

examples.title: Semantics plus a live announcement
examples.code:
{{ status() }}

@if (errors().length) {
    @for (e of errors(); track e) {
  • {{ e }}
    • }
}
examples.explanation: A real button gives the keyboard handler, the role and the focus ring; role=status lets the screen reader announce the async result without the user hunting for it.

angular.question: How would you produce an accessibility report for an application?
angular.answer: The report has to be evidence a team can act on, so I scope it before I test: the key journeys first - sign in, search, the main form, the main dialog - rather than every screen. Three passes feed it. Automated: axe-core in the browser or wired into the component tests, Lighthouse, and the angular-eslint accessibility rules in CI, which give repeatable numbers and catch regressions. Manual keyboard pass: tab order, visible focus, no keyboard traps, Escape closing overlays, and every action reachable without a mouse. Screen-reader pass on the journeys, checking names, roles, headings, form errors and live announcements, because a green automated run only proves a fraction of conformance. Then I write each issue up with the page, the WCAG 2.2 criterion, the severity and user impact, the reproduction, evidence, the suggested fix, an owner and a retest status - a missing label on the payment field is not the same severity as a slightly low contrast ratio on a caption. I track it against the agreed target, usually AA, and I state plainly in the report that automated checks passing is not a claim of accessibility; it is a floor.

examples.title: One row of the report
examples.code:
Page:     /employees/new (step 2)
Issue:    Amount input has no accessible name (screen reader reads 'edit text')
Criterion: WCAG 2.2 - 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
Severity: High - blocks a primary task for screen-reader users
Repro:    Tab to the field, inspect accessible name in the a11y tree
Fix:      <label for="amount">Amount</label> + id on the input
Owner:    FE squad 2      Status: Open -> Fixed, retested 14 Mar
examples.explanation: Severity is argued from user impact, not from how easy the fix is, and every row carries enough detail to be verified by someone who was not in the room.

angular.question: Walk me through routing in Angular - how is it configured, and what does the router actually do?
angular.answer: Routing is a URL-to-view mapping. You declare a Routes array where each route points a path at a component, usually through loadComponent so the code is not in the initial bundle, and register it with provideRouter(routes) in the application config. A router-outlet in the root template is the slot the active component renders into, and RouterLink or Router.navigate moves between routes without a full page load. Around that sit the pieces you are asked about: path parameters for identity (/employees/123), query parameters for optional state (?page=2), child routes for nesting, guards to decide whether navigation proceeds, resolvers to prepare data first, router events such as NavigationEnd for analytics or scroll resets, and a wildcard route for anything unmatched. Deep linking only works if the server falls back to index.html for unknown paths, otherwise a refresh on a nested URL 404s. In practice I also add withComponentInputBinding() so route and query parameters arrive as inputs, a custom route reuse strategy or scroll handling only when needed, and a preloading strategy so important lazy routes are fetched while the user is still reading the first page.

examples.title: A route config with parameters, children and a wildcard
examples.explanation: Each lazy entry is a separate chunk fetched on first navigation; the wildcard must be last or it swallows every path.

angular.question: How do you handle errors in an Angular application, including API errors?
angular.answer: I handle errors at the layer that can do something useful about them, and I distinguish expected failures from bugs. At the source - the service - catchError classifies the failure (status 0 is network or CORS, 401 means re-authenticate, 403 means authenticated but not allowed, 404 is a contract problem, 5xx is upstream) and then either hands back fallback data such as of([]) when the screen can degrade gracefully, or rethrows with throwError so the caller decides. At the component level the error becomes state: a signal the template renders as a message with a retry, loading cleared in finalize() so the UI cannot get stuck half-finished, and technical detail kept out of the user-facing text. Interceptors own what is genuinely cross-cutting - a standard error envelope, logging, refresh-and-retry-once on 401 - but I do not swallow every failure there, because a 404 on one endpoint usually needs its own response. Angular's ErrorHandler catches what nothing else did and ships it to monitoring, and the router gives a separate path for a lazy chunk that fails to download. The rule I keep: every error either reaches a human who can act or reaches a log that someone reads.

examples.title: Classify, then rethrow or degrade
examples.explanation: catchError must return an Observable, so you choose: a fallback keeps the stream alive, throwError keeps the failure visible upstream. Splitting those two is the whole decision.

angular.question: What is zone.js, and why does Angular use it?
angular.answer: zone.js is a library that gives JavaScript execution contexts called zones, and it gets there by patching the asynchronous APIs the browser exposes - timers, event listeners, promises, XHR/fetch callbacks - so that it knows when a scheduled piece of async work starts and finishes. Angular used it as its change-detection trigger: because the zone can see every callback settle, the framework no longer had to be told that state might have changed. The developer experience effect was real - you could update a field inside a setTimeout or an event handler and the view refreshed - and the cost was that Angular had to assume any async completion might have changed anything and re-check the tree. Two things are worth being precise about. First, zone.js is not change detection: it reports that asynchronous work settled, and Angular's change detection decides what to inspect. Second, it is no longer required - the zoneless model, the default for new applications since Angular 21, drops the patching entirely and schedules checks from explicit triggers such as a signal a template reads being written, a listener firing, or markForCheck(). So I would describe it as the mechanism Angular needed before signals made the framework aware of changes at the source.

examples.title: What the zone was standing in for
examples.explanation: Same behaviour, different source of truth about when to render: an intercepted callback versus an explicit signal write.

angular.question: What does cross-browser compatibility mean for an Angular app, and what has zone.js got to do with it?
angular.answer: Cross-browser compatibility means the application behaves acceptably on every browser you have promised to support, and it is a testing and tooling problem, not a framework feature. My approach: agree the support matrix first, because that decides everything else; write standards-based HTML, CSS and JavaScript rather than vendor-specific behaviour; let the TypeScript target and the browserslist configuration downlevel syntax and styles for that matrix; add a polyfill only where a supported browser is genuinely missing a runtime API, which in a modern matrix is rare and always costs bytes; use feature detection at the edges rather than sniffing user agents; and actually run the key journeys in the supported browsers, real devices for the mobile ones or a service such as BrowserStack, with Playwright projects per browser where it is worth automating. Responsive layout, font rendering and input differences (touch versus hover, focus behaviour) are part of it too. zone.js belongs to a completely different category: it is Angular's mechanism for noticing that asynchronous work finished so change detection can run. It has no bearing on whether a browser supports a CSS feature or a JavaScript API, and it is not a compatibility layer - a very common mix-up worth correcting in the answer.

examples.title: The three places compatibility is actually configured
examples.explanation: Syntax, styles and missing APIs are three different problems with three different settings. zone.js is none of them - it is a change-detection dependency you either load or do not.

angular.question: What are polyfills in Angular, and how do you decide which ones you need?
angular.answer: A polyfill supplies at runtime an API a browser does not implement, which is different from transpilation: a transpiler rewrites newer syntax into older syntax, while a polyfill fills in a missing function or behaviour such as a missing navigator or a missing string method. In Angular, polyfills are declared as a build option - angular.json's build.options.polyfills array, where an application running with zones lists 'zone.js' - rather than imported from a hand-maintained polyfills.ts file, which older projects still have. The decision process is short: look at the support matrix, check each candidate feature against it, and add a polyfill only if a browser you must support is actually missing it. I verify with a tool such as caniuse or MDN rather than habit, because the common failure is a copied polyfill list from a project that supported IE11 years ago, silently costing critical-path bytes on every load. I also keep transpilation and polyfills separate in the answer: if the build fails or the syntax breaks it is a target problem, if a function is undefined at runtime it is a polyfill problem. This application needs none of its own, because it is zoneless and targets ES2022 browsers.

examples.title: Where a polyfill lives today
examples.explanation: The array is the whole mechanism now: each entry is a module bundled into the app, so every entry is a kilobyte you have justified.

angular.question: What testing setup does an Angular project get by default?
angular.answer: Historically the CLI scaffolded Karma as the runner and Jasmine as the assertion library: Karma launched a browser, reported results back, and specs used describe/it/expect with spies. Karma was deprecated in 2023 and from Angular 21 the default ng test runs Vitest through the builder, which keeps the familiar Jasmine-style API but runs fast in a DOM environment instead of driving a browser, and it is what this project uses. End-to-end is deliberately not chosen for you: Protractor reached end of life in 2023 and the CLI now asks you to pick from Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO, Puppeteer or Nightwatch. Beyond the tooling, the part of the answer that matters is how I write tests: exercise behaviour rather than implementation - create the fixture, set inputs with setInput, drive an event, then assert on what the user can see; fake services instead of hitting HTTP, using provideHttpClientTesting and the testing controller to verify the method, URL and body; and assert the failure path as well as the happy one, because the empty and error states are where the bugs hide. I would rather have ten tests that would fail if behaviour changed than fifty that only prove the framework works.

examples.title: A component test in the current default setup
examples.explanation: describe/it/expect come from the runner (Vitest here), the service is a spy so nothing hits the network, and the assertion is on the rendered DOM rather than on component fields.

angular.question: What happens when a component is destroyed, and what do you have to clean up?
angular.answer: Angular calls ngOnDestroy once when the component instance is being torn down, and it is the last place you can undo everything the component started. The checklist I run through: long-lived subscriptions (the modern answer is takeUntilDestroyed() in the injection context, or the async pipe in the template, so there is nothing to unsubscribe by hand), intervals and timeouts, event listeners you added yourself, anything you appended to the DOM outside Angular's knowledge, third-party widgets you instantiated, and native resources such as a WebSocket or an observer. Signals blur the line usefully: an effect() created in the component's injection context disposes itself with the component, toSignal() is tied to DestroyRef, and a finite HTTP observable completes on its own so it needs no cleanup at all - the mistake is treating every observable as if it needs an unsubscribe. In tests I prove teardown rather than assume it: assert that ngOnDestroy ran, or that a stopped interval no longer ticks. Worth knowing if you touch a legacy AngularJS codebase: the equivalent is the scope's $destroy event, and AngularJS fires it twice - once broadcast to descendant scopes, once on the element itself when it is removed - so those handlers have to be idempotent.

examples.title: Tear down what the framework cannot
examples.explanation: Angular owns its own subscriptions now; anything it did not create - a raw interval, a listener, a widget - still has to be released in onDestroy, exactly once.

angular.question: How do you integrate a REST API into an Angular application?
angular.answer: I keep HTTP in a typed service per resource and never in a component: register provideHttpClient() once in the application config, then a service injects HttpClient and exposes methods that return an Observable typed to the response shape. The component owns state - loading, data, error as signals - and the service owns the wire. Around that I do four things consistently. Interceptors attach what is cross-cutting: the Authorization header, a correlation id, a consistent error envelope. Unsubscribing matters: because an HttpClient observable cancels on unsubscribe, search-style calls go through switchMap and everything else is tied to the component with takeUntilDestroyed. Validation happens at the boundary, because a TypeScript interface disappears at runtime and does not check the JSON that actually arrived - for anything that drives logic I narrow the payload before trusting it. And where two screens ask for the same collection, I deduplicate with shareReplay rather than firing the request twice. For testing I swap in provideHttpClientTesting, assert the method, URL and body with the testing controller, and drive success, 404 and 500 through the same spec, so the loading and error states are proven rather than hoped for.

examples.title: A resource service and the test that pins its contract
examples.explanation: The spec is a contract test: if someone changes the URL or the method, the test fails before any screen does.

angular.question: A feature runs on the traditional NgRx Store and the team wants to move it to SignalStore. How do you decide whether to do it, and how would you run the migration?
angular.answer: I would decide before I design, because the honest first answer is often 'not yet'. The Store earns its boilerplate when state is shared widely, when you need effects as a visible side-effect stream, devtools time-trace debugging, or rules about what may write. SignalStore wins when the state belongs to one feature, the consumers are already signal-based, and the cost of dispatching actions through reducers is buying nothing. So the first task is to write down the pain - is it boilerplate, test setup, or the indirection of dispatch-then-select - and check how much of the ecosystem the feature actually relies on. If it is app-wide state with ten consumers and middleware, I would keep the Store and improve it instead. If it is a feature slice, I migrate in a way that keeps a working application at every step: characterise the current behaviour with tests first, so the reducer and effect outcomes are pinned; build the SignalStore slice with withState for the data, withComputed for derived values, withMethods for the actions that used to be dispatched, and withHooks for load and reset; keep the old facade - the same selectors and dispatch points - so nothing outside the feature notices; then move consumers one component at a time from store.select to a signal and from dispatch to a method call. The last step deletes the actions, reducers and effects for that slice, and the two models coexist until then. The risks I would name out loud: two sources of truth if both stores write the same data during the transition, losing the devtools timeline the team relied on, and a team learning a new pattern mid-delivery. Migrating because SignalStore is newer is not a reason.

examples.title: The slice that replaces an actions/reducers/effects trio
examples.explanation: state replaces the reducer, computed replaces the memoized selector, methods replace dispatch, and the HTTP call sits where the effect used to - one file where there were three, with no dispatcher in between.

performance.question: What happens when a user types a URL into the browser and presses enter?
performance.answer:
The first question of this category, and the one that reveals whether you actually
understand the network or just the framework. Walk it in order without
skipping: URL parsing, DNS resolution to an IP, TCP connection, TLS handshake,
the HTTP request, the response, and then what the browser does with the bytes. Two
details that separate a strong answer from a recited one: DNS and TLS both happen
before any application code runs, and for a single-page app the server usually
returns the same index.html for every route - so the router, not the server,
decides what the user sees. Mention HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 multiplexing, and be honest
about what you have measured versus what you know generally.

examples.title: Full request path to first render
examples.code:
DNS
User types app.example.com/orders/42
  -> URL parsed: scheme, host, path
  -> DNS resolution: hostname -> IP (cached by browser, OS, or resolver)

TCP
  -> TCP handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK

TLS
  -> TLS 1.3 handshake, certificates verified
  -> If resuming a previous connection, this is much cheaper

HTTP
  -> GET /orders/42 HTTP/2
  -> CDN or server replies. For a SPA the response is almost always the same
     index.html regardless of the /orders/42 path - the server does not know
     or care which route you wanted.

Browser
  -> HTML received, parsing starts immediately, streaming
  -> Preload scanner scans ahead for CSS, JS, images and starts fetching
  -> Render-blocking CSS found in <head> pauses first paint
  -> <script type="module"> is deferred by default, so it does not block
     parsing, but DOMContentLoaded waits for module execution

What a candidate often gets wrong:
"the root component runs first."
No. The first application code to run is whatever main.ts imports. The root
component class - App in app.ts, or AppComponent in older projects - is a
class declaration, and nothing instantiates it until bootstrapApplication is
called from main.ts.
examples.explanation:
Differentiating DNS/TCP/TLS from HTTP, and being clear that the server returns the
same HTML for every route, are the two markers of a real answer.

performance.question: Walk me through how an Angular app boots, step by step. Does it go to app.ts first?
performance.answer:
No - and correcting that misconception inside the answer is valuable, because it
tests whether you know the order rather than the file names. The order is: the
browser receives index.html, discovers the module script, downloads and executes
main.ts, main.ts calls bootstrapApplication with a root component, Angular creates
that component, its template renders, and only then does anything user-visible
appear. Behind the scenes, the build tool read the main property in angular.json
(which points at src/main.ts) and the Angular CLI injected the compiled bundle
scripts near the bottom of index.html, which is why main-XYZ.js is the first
application code to run. The root component class is inert until
bootstrapApplication instantiates it and renders it into the <app-root> placeholder. Within that you should be able to name where the router fits: the root template
contains router-outlet, the router reads the current URL, matches it against the
route config, and for a lazy route triggers a dynamic import before the routed
component is created. Mention that in Angular 21+ this app is zoneless by default,
so change detection is scheduled by notification rather than by zone.js. Two details that separate a real answer from the file names: bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig) assembles the root injector from appConfig's providers - provideRouter, provideHttpClient and every app-wide service - before the root component is created, so anything the first render depends on belongs there; and the root component stays a shell until the router matches the URL and renders the routed component into router-outlet, which is why a slow first route feels like a slow application.

index.html (build output)

  <html lang="en">
    <head>
      <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles-ABC.css">   <!-- render-blocking -->
    </head>
    <body>
      <app-root></app-root>
      <script type="module" src="main-XYZ.js"></script>
    </body>
  </html>

main.ts
  import { bootstrapApplication } from '@angular/platform-browser';
  import { App } from './app/app';
  import { appConfig } from './app/app.config';

  bootstrapApplication(App, appConfig)
    .catch((err) => console.error(err));

app.ts  (NOT the entry point - the class only)
  @Component({
    selector: 'app-root',
    imports: [RouterOutlet],
    template: `<router-outlet />`,
  })
  export class App {}

The actual order
  1. HTML parsed, app-root element exists as an empty host element
  2. main.js downloaded, module graph resolved
  3. main.ts executes -> bootstrapApplication(App, appConfig)
  4. Angular creates App and renders its template into <app-root>
  5. Router initialises, reads location.pathname
  6. Route matched. If the route is lazy:
       loadComponent: () => import('./orders/orders.component')
     -> dynamic import of that chunk -> network request -> then component created
  7. First meaningful paint of real content

Note on file names
  Angular 20+ generates src/app/app.ts exporting App rather than
  src/app/app.component.ts exporting AppComponent. Either way the logic is the
  same - the root component is not the entry point, main.ts is.

Key point
  Nothing renders until step 4 at the earliest, and nothing route-specific renders
  until step 6. Both are network-bound, not CPU-bound, which is why this is a
  performance question.
examples.explanation:
Naming the exact order, correcting the root-component misconception explicitly, and
placing the router dynamic import at the right step is what a strong answer looks
like.

performance.question: How does the browser decide what to fetch from your index.html, and in what order?
performance.answer:
Tests whether you know there is a real parser and a separate preload scanner. The
browser parses HTML incrementally, and the preload scanner runs ahead of the DOM
parser looking for things it can fetch early - stylesheets, scripts, images, fonts.
That is why a script far down the body can already be downloading. Then the priority
rules kick in: CSS in head is render-blocking, module scripts are deferred so they do
not block parsing but do gate DOMContentLoaded, and async scripts have no ordering
guarantee. Fonts are lazy by default, so they only start once something needs them.
Practical consequences: preloading a file the preload scanner would have found anyway
wastes bandwidth, and script tags placed in body get discovered later unless they are
module or defer.

examples.title: Parser, preload scanner, and priority
examples.code: Parsing HTML is parsed incrementally. The DOM is built as bytes arrive, which is why streaming SSR can show content before the response finishes. Preload scanner Runs ahead of the DOM parser specifically to find fetchable resources early: high priority, render-blocking
examples.explanation:
Distinguishing the DOM parser from the preload scanner, knowing that module scripts
are deferred, and understanding that img discovery does not depend on width/height.

performance.question: What is code splitting in an Angular app, and how does a lazy route actually load?
performance.answer:
The mechanism to be precise about: the build tool reads the dynamic import in the
route configuration, puts that component and its unique dependencies in a separate
chunk, and leaves it out of the initial bundle. At runtime the router triggers the
import, which is just a promise-returning network fetch, and only after it
resolves is the component created. The important performance consequence is that
lazy loading moves bytes off the critical path rather than making them smaller,
and it costs you a round trip on first navigation - so prefetching is the usual
follow-up. Be able to explain why a barrel file can defeat splitting, because
importing one symbol from a barrel can drag the whole barrel into the chunk
graph. A few details worth knowing rather than assuming: a lazy component does not automatically get a chunk of its own, because dependencies shared with other routes are extracted into shared chunks; a chunk the browser has already cached costs no round trip on a later visit; and the only way to confirm what actually happened is to read the production build's chunk list and watch the network waterfall on a first navigation, rather than trusting the route config.

examples.title: Dynamic import in the route config
examples.explanation:
Lazy loading moves work off the critical path rather than reducing it, and the
barrel-file explanation is what shows you understand the build, not just the API.

performance.question: What are render-blocking resources, how do you find them, and how do you fix them?
performance.answer:
Render-blocking means the browser cannot paint until the resource is parsed, so it
directly caps First Contentful Paint. In Angular you should know that the CLI already
does the main optimisation for you: the application builder inlines critical CSS by
default, so the classic manual critical-CSS dance is usually not something you write
yourself. What is left for you is knowing what it cannot do - it cannot help with
third-party tags, it does not apply to inline styles in templates, and you may need
to disable or tune it. Also know the trade-off: inlining removes a round trip but
grows the HTML and cannot be cached across pages, and a single render-blocking
stylesheet blocks everything no matter how small it is.

examples.title: Angular already inlines critical CSS - what is left for you
examples.code:
What the CLI does for you by default

  // angular.json -> build -> configurations -> production
  "optimization": {
    "scripts": true,
    "styles": {
      "minify": true,
      "inlineCritical": true,     // <-- default, uses Beasties
      "removeSpecialComments": true
    },
    "fonts": true
  }

  "optimization" itself defaults to true, so a production build gets this without
  you configuring anything.

What that means in practice
  The build extracts the CSS needed for first paint and inlines it into index.html.
  The rest is loaded as a normal stylesheet. So if you are writing an interview
  answer about manual critical CSS in an Angular app, the strong version starts by
  saying the tooling already handles it.

What it cannot do for you

  1. Third-party tags - analytics, chat widgets, consent banners
       <script async src="analytics.js"></script>
       <script defer src="support-widget.js"></script>
       These are not part of your CSS graph at all.

  2. Inline styles in templates, and styles added at runtime.

  3. The case where critical CSS inlining is wrong for you. If your critical CSS is
     large, or the page structure varies a lot per route, inlining bloats the HTML
     and you would rather disable it:
       "optimization": { "styles": { "inlineCritical": false } }
     then load styles yourself.

Why it matters anyway
  A single render-blocking stylesheet blocks first paint for a full round trip, no
  matter how small it is. That is the property to be able to explain.
examples.explanation:
Knowing inlineCritical defaults to true is the Angular-specific fact that makes the
answer credible; the remaining blockers are third-party tags, not your own CSS.

performance.question: What are Core Web Vitals, and how do you measure and diagnose each one?
performance.answer:
Three metrics that approximate real user experience, which means the field data
matters as much as the lab data. Know what each measures and, more importantly,
what each diagnosis is: LCP is about whether the main content arrives fast, so
look at server response, render-blocking resources and image priority; INP is
about whether the main thread is free when the user acts, so look at long tasks
and expensive handlers; CLS is about whether things move after they appear, so
look at images without dimensions, web fonts swapping in, and content injected
above existing content. The graded detail is being able to distinguish a lab score
from field data and to say which one you would optimise against.

examples.title: Metric, threshold, and what to actually look at
examples.code:
LCP - Largest Contentful Paint
  Measures when the largest element finished painting.
  Good under 2.5s (75th percentile).
  Diagnose: server response time, render-blocking CSS, whether the LCP element
  is an image with lazy loading applied by mistake, font blocking paint.

INP - Interaction to Next Paint
  Measures the latency from a user interaction to the next frame.
  Good under 200ms. This replaced First Input Delay - it measures the whole
  interaction, not just the first one.
  Diagnose: long tasks, heavy event handlers, expensive re-renders, layout
  thrash where you read and write layout properties in a loop.

CLS - Cumulative Layout Shift
  Measures unexpected movement of visible content.
  Good under 0.1.
  Diagnose: images and iframes without width/height, web fonts swapping after
  fallback text is painted, ads or banners inserted above existing content,
  async content pushing content down.

Lab vs field
  Lab (Lighthouse, DevTools, WebPageTest): one device, one network, repeatable.
  Field (CrUX, RUM): real devices on real networks, includes the users you
  care least about and most about.

  I optimise against field data and use the lab to reproduce. A lab score can
  be perfect while field INP is bad, because a lab run never does the sequence
  of interactions a real user does.
examples.explanation:
Connecting each metric to a concrete diagnostic, and explicitly preferring field
data, is what a senior answer does. Reciting the thresholds is not enough.

performance.question: What is a long task, and how does blocking the main thread show up to a user?
performance.answer:
A long task is any script execution over roughly 50ms, and the number is not
arbitrary - it is the point at which the browser cannot reliably keep up with input
handling and rendering. The user-visible symptoms are input lag, animations that
stutter, and INP going up, all of which are the same root cause. The important
distinction for an Angular developer is between work that is long but interruptible
and work that is long and blocking: chunking work with the scheduler or yielding
between frames can make an acceptable task into a fine one, whereas anything inside
a synchronous loop that touches DOM layout will block no matter how you slice it.

examples.title: Long task, and the yield that fixes it
examples.explanation: The 50ms threshold, the same root cause behind input lag and INP, and knowing that yielding only fixes interruptible work - not a 10k-row DOM problem. Angular ships no scheduler.yield(), so use setTimeout or a MessageChannel, not a microtask.

performance.question: How do you profile an Angular app and find out what is actually slow?
performance.answer:
Method, not tool names, is the grade. The sequence that works: reproduce
consistently, measure before changing anything, find the longest task or the
largest cost, and only then optimise - then re-measure to confirm. On top of
that, know the Angular-specific tools: the DevTools Performance panel for the
main thread, the Angular profiler (or the newer DevTools performance extension
features) for change detection, and heap snapshots for retained memory. A strong
answer includes a case where a profiler contradicted the team belief - that is
what proves you measured rather than assumed.

examples.title: Reproduce, measure, confirm
examples.code:
Step 1 - reproduce it consistently
  A vague "it feels slow" cannot be optimised. Record a scripted interaction
  with the same data volume every time.

Step 2 - measure before touching anything
  DevTools -> Performance:
    - record the interaction
    - look at the summary donut first: scripting vs rendering vs painting
    - the longest task, then what dominates inside it

  Angular-specific:
    - the profiler shows change detection runs and their cost
    - a slow screen is often 40ms of change detection across 3000 views, not
      one slow function

  Network: check whether it was actually a 900ms API call

Step 3 - the finding that contradicted the team
  The team believed a third-party chart library was the problem.
  The profile showed 12ms in the chart library and 380ms in a change
  detection pass, caused by a computed property that returned a new array
  identity on every read and therefore invalidated OnPush children.

Step 4 - fix and re-measure
  Memoise the array so the identity is stable. Re-record: change detection
  dropped from 380ms to 20ms. The chart library stayed.

For memory: take a heap snapshot, do the interaction 5 times, take another,
sort by retained size, and look for detached DOM trees - that is the signature
of a leak.
examples.explanation:
Reproduce-measure-confirm as a sequence, knowing the Angular profiler is about
change detection rather than functions, and telling a story where measurement
contradicted the team belief.

performance.question: How does change detection affect Angular performance, and what are the ways to reduce its cost?
performance.answer:
Be precise about the mechanism, because this is where vague answers fall apart.
Change detection walks a tree of components and evaluates bindings. In a zoneless
app it does not run on a timer or on every event; it is scheduled when Angular
notices something that needs rendering - a signal written that a template reads, an
input set, a host or template listener firing, markForCheck, or a view being
attached. That is notification-based, so the wins come from not doing unnecessary
work rather than from the scheduler being faster. Know that this is the default in
Angular 21+, and that zone.js apps still exist and still tick on async events, which
is why the two behave differently. The levers are OnPush, pure pipes, stable keys,
and running genuinely framework-free code outside Angular when it does not need to
touch the DOM.

examples.title: Zoneless scheduling, and the levers
examples.code:
How scheduling works without zone.js
  With zone.js, any patched event, timer, or promise resolution triggered a full
  tick. Without it, Angular schedules change detection when it observes one of:
    - a signal that is read in a template is written
    - ComponentRef.setInput
    - a bound host or template listener fires
    - ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck
    - a view marked dirty is attached, or removed

  This is the default in Angular 21+. In v20 you opted in with
  provideZonelessChangeDetection(). Your own app has no zone.js dependency at all,
  so it is already in this mode.

Lever 1 - OnPush
  @Component({ changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush })
  export class OrderListComponent {}
  With zoneless, OnPush still matters: it stops a parent invalidation from cascading
  into children that read nothing you changed. Caveat: a new array or object identity
  defeats it.

Lever 2 - pure pipes (already the default)
  {{ total | currency }}                              // memoised on total
  {{ total | currency: 'GBP' : 'symbol' : '1.2-2' }}   // memoised on total + args
  transform() runs only when an argument changes by ===, so the thing to avoid is an
  impure pipe (pure: false), which re-runs on every change detection pass

Lever 3 - stable keys
  @for (row of rows(); track row.id) { ... }      // stable
  @for (row of rows(); track $index) { ... }      // defeats the diff
  Without a stable key Angular recreates the DOM and loses focus, scroll and state.

Lever 4 - do less
  The real win is not doing the work. 3000 rows of Material table is the problem;
  virtualisation beats any scheduler tweak.

Lever 5 - stay out of the framework entirely
  If your code only touches the DOM and never changes component state, do not run
  it through Angular at all:
    private readonly zone = inject(NgZone);

    ngAfterViewInit(): void {
      this.zone.runOutsideAngular(() => {
        element.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll);  // no CD triggered
      });
    }
examples.explanation:
Knowing the zoneless scheduling triggers as a specific list, understanding it is
the v21+ default, and using NgZone.runOutsideAngular for pure DOM work rather than
claiming a bare function "runs outside Angular".

performance.question: What is tree shaking, and how do you verify that it is actually working rather than assuming it?
performance.answer:
This is the verify-it follow-up to the basic definition. Tree shaking removes
exports nothing imports, and it is easy to claim and hard to confirm. The
mechanisms are sideEffects metadata so the bundler knows a file has no
import-time side effects, static versus dynamic imports, and module format -
CommonJS modules cannot be statically analysed, so one require-style dependency can
defeat the whole thing. Verification is the graded part: look at the actual chunk
contents in the build output or the DevTools network panel rather than trusting the
build summary, and know that barrel files, CommonJS interop and accidental
side-effect imports are the usual leaks.

examples.title: Verify, do not assume
examples.code:
The setup
  package.json
  {
    "sideEffects": false
  }
  Tells the bundler every file in this package is safe to drop if unused. If you
  have any import-time side effect (polyfills, CSS imports, registering something
  global), list them:
  "sideEffects": ["*.css", "./src/polyfills.ts"]

Why it fails silently
  1. CommonJS. A dependency shipping CJS cannot be statically analysed, so the whole
     module is kept:
       import moment from 'moment';        // the entire library
       import { debounce } from 'lodash';  // unless you use lodash-es or a
                                           // per-method import
  2. Barrel files. import { thing } from './utils' forces the bundler to analyse
     ./utils/index.ts, which may re-export 40 things.
  3. Accidental side-effect import:
       import './polyfills';   // kept even if nothing is used

Verification
  npx ng build --configuration production
  Look at the output table - lazy chunks in kB, and the initial total.

  Then confirm rather than trust:
    - DevTools -> Network -> the JS files actually fetched on a cold load
    - Sources panel -> the bundle, search for a symbol you think is unused
    - source-map-explorer or rollup-plugin-visualizer to attribute bundle size to
      specific files

  I found 180kb of moment this way. The fix was replacing it, not configuring the
  bundler harder.
examples.explanation:
Knowing CJS defeats shaking, that sideEffects is a contract you must not lie about,
and verifying against the network panel rather than the build summary.

performance.question: What are the usual causes of a slow Angular app, and how do you prioritise which one to fix?
performance.answer:
Good answers are a prioritisation framework rather than a list, because the list is
easy to recite. The useful ordering is by cost of fix against cost of delay: fix
network-bound work first, because it is usually both the biggest and the easiest -
a 900ms API call dwarfs any template optimisation. Then main-thread blocking,
because it affects every interaction. Then rendering volume, because it is
proportional and grows with the product. Then bundle size, which matters most on
first load on bad networks and barely at all once cached. The thing that
distinguishes a senior answer is naming what you deliberately did not fix and
why, and saying how you decided where to stop.

examples.title: Rank by cost of fix against cost of delay
examples.code:
Ranked for a typical internal app with 40k users on office wifi:

1. Network-bound, before anything else
   An 800ms API call on the critical path. Fix is often a cache or a
   prefetch, and the win is measured in hundreds of ms.
   Highest ratio of gain to effort of anything on this list.

2. Main-thread blocking
   Long tasks over 50ms. Affects every interaction, so it hurts INP directly.
   Usually needs scheduler.yield or moving work out of the change detection
   path.

3. Rendering volume
   500-row Material table with filtering and sorting on every keystroke.
   Fix: virtualisation, and debouncing the filter so it is not per keystroke.

4. Bundle size
   Only matters for first load on poor networks. If 80% of sessions are repeat
   and the bundle is cached, this is near zero and should be last.

5. Change detection cost
   Often real but rarely the biggest single item. Fix with OnPush and signals.

What I deliberately did not fix
  We spent two days on bundle size - the app was 900kb - and our field LCP was
  already fine because 95% of traffic was repeat visits served from cache. I
  should have checked the field data before optimising. We kept maybe 5% of that
  work.
examples.explanation:
Ranking with a stated reason, and naming work you chose not to do and why, is what
separates this from a recited list.

performance.question: An Angular app's memory grows steadily in production as users navigate between routes. How do you track down what is retaining the memory?
performance.answer:
This is the diagnostic question, as opposed to the leak question - the graded part
is distinguishing a real leak from a cache that is behaving correctly, which is
where most investigations go wrong. The method that works is comparison rather
