than inspection: take a heap snapshot, repeat the suspect interaction several
times, force GC, take another, and diff. A real leak grows monotonically with each
repetition, whereas lazy route chunks and caches plateau. Learn to read the
dominators tree, because the retaining object is usually held by a closure you
cannot see at the call site. In Angular the causes are almost always one of three:
an unsubscribed subscription, a listener or timer registered outside Angular, or a
reference to a detached DOM node.

examples.title: Snapshot, repeat, diff
examples.code:
The three causes
  1. Subscription never unsubscribed
       items$ = new Subject();
     // subscribed in a component that can be destroyed
  2. Listener or timer outside Angular
     setInterval(() => this.poll(), 5000);   // survives the component
  3. Detached DOM
     A closure holds a reference to a node the framework has already removed.
     9,912 detached nodes, one detached HTMLDivElement.

The method
  1. DevTools -> Memory -> Heap snapshot
  2. Perform the suspect interaction - navigate to a route with a chart, back, five
     times
  3. Force GC, then take snapshot 2
  4. Comparison view, sort by retained size

The distinction that matters
  Detached node count climbing with each repetition is a leak.
  Lazy route chunks staying resident after the first load are cached, not leaking -
    they plateau. Confusing these two is why people either fix non-problems or miss
    real ones.

Finding the actual retainer
  Select the leaking object, expand the dominators tree, and follow it down. In one
  case the retainer was an arrow function passed to a subscribe-like library API,
  which held the destroyed component forever. You will not find this at the call
  site; the retainer and the leak are in different places.

Prevention, once you have diagnosed it
  import { takeUntilDestroyed } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';

  private readonly destroyRef = inject(DestroyRef);

  ngOnInit(): void {
    this.timer$
      .pipe(takeUntilDestroyed(this.destroyRef))
      .subscribe(() => this.tick());
  }
examples.explanation:
The snapshot-and-diff method, knowing that plateauing chunk memory is a cache
rather than a leak, and reading the dominators tree to find the retainer.

performance.question: What is the difference between initial load, a reload, and a route transition? How should each be measured?
performance.answer:
They have completely different bottlenecks, and optimising the wrong one is a
classic mistake. The initial load has nothing cached, so it is dominated by network
round trips and parse cost - this is where bundle size, render-blocking resources
and the number of requests matter. A reload has the browser HTTP cache partly
warm but not necessarily the runtime state, so it is dominated by parse and
execute time - code cache and bundle size matter more than request count. A route
transition happens inside a running app with the framework already loaded, so it
is dominated by data fetching and rendering work, and bundle size is almost
irrelevant. Being able to separate them is the whole point of the question.

examples.title: Three different bottlenecks
examples.code:
Initial load (cold)
  Cache: empty. Server: cold or warm.
  Dominated by: round trips, render-blocking resources, parse time.
  Measure: Lighthouse, throttled to Slow 4G, with cache disabled.
  Fixes that matter: fewer requests, code splitting, deferring below-fold work.

Reload (browser cache warm)
  JS may come from HTTP cache; the runtime state is gone.
  Dominated by: parse and execute, V8 compile, hydration work.
  Measure: same tools but with the cache enabled, and look at the total
  scripting time rather than the request waterfall.

Route transition (SPA, app already running)
  Framework loaded, no new initial bundle.
  Dominated by: the API call for the route data, and rendering the new view.
  Measure: in-app marks around the navigation, and the DevTools Network panel
  filtered by XHR - not the document request.
  Fixes that matter: query caching, pagination, virtualisation, OnPush.

The mistake
  "Our bundle is 1.4mb so the app is slow."
  For a user on their fifth navigation that number is irrelevant. Split the
  complaint into which of the three it is before touching anything.
examples.explanation:
Separating cold-load network cost from reload parse cost from route-transition
rendering cost, and knowing which fixes apply to which.

performance.question: How do prefetching and preloading differ, and when is either worth it?
performance.answer:
Prefetch is for resources you expect to need soon but which must not block anything
now; preload is for resources you know you need immediately, fetched at high
priority and consumed straight away. The distinction matters because a preload on
something the preload scanner would have found anyway is pure loss - it competes
for bandwidth and the browser warns you about it. In Angular, route prefetching is
the standard win because the routes are known ahead of time, so the trade is
bandwidth against first-navigation latency. Know that RouterLink has no prefetch
input and that preloading is configured at the router provider level, not on a link.

examples.title: Prefetch vs preload, and how Angular route preloading is actually configured
examples.explanation:
The discoverability rule for preloads, that RouterLink has no prefetch input and
preloading is configured via withPreloading, and that PreloadAllModules is stable
rather than deprecated.

performance.question: How does a service worker change loading performance, and what are the risks?
performance.answer:
The service worker sits between the network and the app and can serve from a
cache, which turns a network-bound first load into a cache-bound one for repeat
visits. That is a large win for returning users on bad networks and it is also
the source of the classic failure: a stale app shell served to a user whose
JavaScript chunks have been evicted, producing a version mismatch errors. Any
answer should mention versioned caches and cleanup on activate. Be honest that it
adds a layer of complexity and a failure mode that does not exist without one,
and that for a frequently updated internal app it may not be worth it.

examples.title: Caching strategies and the failure mode
examples.code:
Lifecycle
  install  -> precache the shell
  activate -> delete old caches by version
  fetch    -> serve from cache, then update in the background

Angular service worker
  npx ng add @angular/pwa
  ngsw-config.json:
  {
    "index": "/index.html",
    "assetGroups": [
      {
        "name": "app",
        "installMode": "prefetch",
        "resources": { "files": ["/favicon.ico", "/*.css", "/*.js"] }
      }
    ],
    "navigationRequestStrategy": "performance",
    "navigationUrls": ["/**", "!/**/*.*", "!/**/*__*", "!/**/*__*/**"]
  }

The failure that bites everyone
  index.html is cached, but a lazily loaded chunk from the new deployment has
  not been fetched yet and the old one has been evicted. The browser gets a
  404 for the chunk hash that index.html asked for.

  Fix: version the cache name, delete old caches on activate, and do not cache
  hashed chunk requests with a cache-first strategy - let them go to the
  network, the browser HTTP cache is usually enough.

Is it worth it here?
  For a public app with returning users, yes. For an internal app that deploys
  weekly to a few hundred people, the complexity is probably not paying for
  itself - the browser HTTP cache already covers most of the repeat-visit case.
examples.explanation:
Naming the version-mismatch failure, cache versioning and cleanup on activate,
and being willing to say the service worker is not worth it for your app.

performance.question: How do fonts and images affect performance, and how do you load them well?
performance.answer:
Both affect Core Web Vitals in specific ways, which is what makes this a
performance question rather than a styling one. Fonts: a late-arriving web font
causes a flash of invisible text and then a layout shift as the real font replaces
the fallback, so the fix is a size-matched fallback face with metric overrides on
the fallback, not on the web font itself. Images: an image without intrinsic
dimensions causes layout shift when it loads, and a lazy-loaded LCP element is a
direct LCP regression. The practical skills are sizing attributes, responsive
sources, fetchpriority on the LCP image, and preloading exactly one LCP image rather
than several candidates.

examples.title: Fonts and images, tied to CLS and LCP
examples.explanation:
Putting metric overrides on the fallback face rather than the web font, and the
specific error of lazy-loading the LCP image, are the details that stand out.

performance.question: What is the difference between a dev build and a production build in Angular, and why does only one of them tell you about performance?
performance.answer:
Several switches are on in production, and being able to name what each changes is
the grade. Correct one common misconception first: AOT has been the default since
Angular 9, so both ng serve and ng build compile ahead of time, and JIT is
effectively only something you encounter in TestBed. What production actually
changes is minification and mangling, tree shaking, budget enforcement, font and
critical-CSS inlining, and output hashing. The practical point that matters: dev
builds enable extra runtime error checking that production strips, so a dev build is
both slower and a different program - which is why performance measured on ng serve
is meaningless.

examples.title: What each production switch changes
examples.code:
package.json / angular.json
  "configurations": {
    "production": {
      "optimization": {
        "scripts": true,          // minify + mangle
        "styles": { "minify": true, "inlineCritical": true },
        "fonts": true
      },
      "budgets": [
        { "type": "initial", "maximumWarning": "500kB", "maximumError": "1MB" },
        { "type": "anyComponentStyle", "maximumWarning": "4kB", "maximumError": "8kB" }
      ],
      "outputHashing": "all",
      "sourceMap": false
    }
  }

About AOT specifically
  "aot" defaults to true. It has done since Angular 9, so this is not a production-only
  switch. ng serve also compiles AOT. JIT survives in TestBed, which is why test
  environments can behave differently from a production build.

What production actually changes
  Minification   names mangled, whitespace removed
  Tree shaking   unused code removed, plus "sideEffects": false
  Budgets        CI fails if initial bundle exceeds a limit
  Critical CSS   inlined into index.html
  Output hashing index.html references main-ABC123.js so caches update
  Source maps    off by default in production

Run it and measure the right thing
  npx ng build --configuration production
  npx http-server dist/app/browser -p 8080 --proxy http://localhost:4200

  Then measure this, not ng serve.

  Dev builds add runtime checks that production strips - for example, some template
  diagnostics only run in development mode. The module graph served in development is
  not the graph that ships.
examples.explanation:
Correcting the AOT misconception - it is not a production switch and has been default
since v9 - and listing what production actually changes is the core of this answer.

performance.question: How would you set up bundle budgets, and what happens when one is exceeded?
performance.answer:
The mechanics are easy; the judgement is what is graded. Budgets are declared in
angular.json and enforced at build time - maximumWarning is advisory,
maximumError fails the build. The judgement is picking a number: it should come from
your actual current size plus a small allowance, not from a round number, and you
should cover both the initial bundle and individual lazy chunks, because a 400kb
route chunk fails on first navigation exactly as badly as a large initial bundle
does. The consequence to talk through is what happens when a PR exceeds it: whether
it blocks before merge, whether there is a waiver process, and who approves. A
budget that everyone routinely overrides is worse than no budget, because it is a
signal you have chosen to ignore.

examples.title: Declaring, enforcing, and the override problem
examples.code:
angular.json
  "configurations": {
    "production": {
      "budgets": [
        { "type": "initial", "maximumWarning": "500kB", "maximumError": "1MB" },
        { "type": "anyComponentStyle", "maximumWarning": "4kB", "maximumError": "8kB" },
        { "type": "bundle", "name": "admin", "maximumWarning": "300kB",
          "maximumError": "500kB" }
      ]
    }
  }

Available budget types
  initial            total size of the initial bundle
  bundle             a named bundle - requires an exact name, not a glob
  anyScript          any single script
  allScript          all scripts together
  any                any single asset
  all                everything
  anyComponentStyle  a single component stylesheet

Note the units: kB and MB, capital B. This is the same casing the CLI uses and it
is what the docs show - kb is not accepted.

Where the number comes from
  Not a round number someone liked. It is our current initial bundle plus about
  10%. Starting at exactly current size would block legitimate work; starting at a
  round 500kB when we are at 900kB is theatre.

Per-bundle budget matters too
  A 400kb lazy chunk fails on first navigation just as badly as a big initial
  bundle, and the initial budget will not catch it. That is what the bundle type with
  a name is for.

When a PR exceeds it
  maximumError fails the build, so the decision is made before merge rather than
  discovered in production.

  We require a waiver with a named reason and an owner to remove an existing budget
  temporarily. It happens maybe once a quarter.

  What I would not do: raise the budget silently in the same PR. That is how a budget
  stops meaning anything.

Failure mode to avoid
  Three waivers in a month and people stop reading the warnings. At that point the
  budget is decoration.
examples.explanation:
Justifying the number from real data, adding a per-bundle budget as well as initial,
using kB casing, and having an explicit waiver process rather than quietly raising
limits.

performance.question: What is SSR and hydration, in plain terms?
performance.answer: SSR, or server-side rendering, means the server runs your Angular app and sends the browser a fully built HTML page, instead of an almost-empty page that only fills in once JavaScript has loaded. The user sees real content immediately, which is faster on slow connections and much better for search engines. Hydration is the next step. When the JavaScript finally arrives in the browser, Angular does not throw that HTML away and render everything again; it attaches to the HTML that is already there, wires up event listeners and makes the page interactive. Reusing the existing markup is the whole point, and it is what the word hydration means. Two things follow from that. First, the server and the browser must produce exactly the same markup, otherwise Angular reports a hydration mismatch. Second, SSR means you now need a Node server in production, and any code that touches window or document has to be guarded so it still runs on the server. That Node server is only the renderer, not a replacement for your backend: your real API (or database) is still there and still involved. The difference is where data is fetched - during the server render an injectable can call HttpClient and bake the result into the HTML, so the first paint already contains the data instead of an empty shell that fetches afterwards. From then on the browser talks to the same backend as before. It is worth it for public, content-heavy pages and SEO; for a dashboard behind a login, plain client-side rendering with good caching is often the better trade.

examples.title: What actually happens, step by step
examples.code:
Without SSR
  Browser downloads a nearly empty index.html -> downloads and runs JS ->
  renders the app -> user finally sees content. First paint waits on JS.

With SSR + hydration
  1. Server renders the components to an HTML string and sends it. It may call
     the real API or database here, so the HTML already carries the data.
  2. Browser paints that HTML right away, before any JS runs.
  3. JS loads; Angular hydrates: it reuses the existing DOM instead of
     recreating it, attaches event listeners and becomes interactive.

So SSR fixes what the user sees first; hydration fixes when it becomes usable.
examples.explanation: SSR is about the first paint; hydration is about turning that server-rendered HTML into a live, interactive app without rebuilding the DOM.

examples.title: Keeping server-only code safe
examples.explanation: Code that runs during SSR has no DOM, so anything touching window or document is wrapped in a platform check to avoid breaking the server render.

performance.question: What does a Performance API measurement look like in practice, and how would you trust it?
performance.answer:
Trust is the graded word. In-app marks are useful for route transitions and slow
interactions, but they only measure your application - not the network, not the
browser parse, and nothing that happens before your code runs, which is where
first-load problems live. So pair them: browser-native measurement for what the user
experiences, application marks for attribution within it. Use performance.mark and
performance.measure from the browser Performance API, not perf_hooks, which is a Node
module and will not resolve in a browser bundle. Also be honest about measurement
overhead and about the difference between a synthetic run and a real user.

examples.title: Two layers of measurement
examples.explanation:
Using performance.mark rather than Node's perf_hooks, stating what in-app marks
cannot see, and using buffered observers is what makes measurement trustworthy.

performance.question: Customers complain the app takes around 8 seconds to load. Walk me through your diagnosis and fix.
performance.answer: Measure the phases with Lighthouse/WebPageTest: is it bundle size, blocking JS, API latency or render? Shrink the bundle with lazy loading of routes and @defer blocks for non-critical widgets, enable build-time optimizations, compress images (NgOptimizedImage), and consider SSR with hydration or prerendering for the first paint. Verify each change against Core Web Vitals instead of guessing.

examples.title: Route-level lazy loading
examples.code: { path: 'reports', loadComponent: () => import('./reports/reports').then(c => c.Reports) }
examples.explanation: Each route ships its own chunk, so first paint only downloads what the landing page needs.

examples.title: Defer the heavy widget
examples.code:
<app-dashboard>
  @defer (on viewport) { <app-revenue-chart /> } @placeholder { <app-skeleton /> }
</app-dashboard>
examples.explanation: @defer splits a component out of the initial bundle and loads it when it becomes visible or on interaction.

performance.question: A page with very large forms and dropdown lists feels sluggish. What do you optimise, and in what order?
performance.answer: Work top-down on cost per change-detection cycle, because that is what sluggishness usually means. First, make sure components are OnPush - with default change detection every keypress re-evaluates every template on the page. Second, kill hidden costs inside those templates: getters, function calls and pipes re-run on every check, so precompute into fields or signals (or make a pipe pure). Third, do not ship data you do not need: a 10k-row dropdown should be a remote search-ahead or virtualized list, not 10k options in the initial payload. Fourth, images go through NgOptimizedImage. Finally, if the remaining work is genuinely CPU-bound (sorting/filtering 100k rows), move it off the main thread instead of micro-optimising templates.

examples.title: OnPush + stable identity in the list
examples.explanation: Getters in templates are a classic hidden cost; a computed caches by dependency.

examples.title: Dropdown: search-ahead instead of shipping 10k options
examples.explanation: Only the visible matches exist in the DOM, so the form has a small working set.

examples.title: Images through NgOptimizedImage
examples.explanation: NgOptimizedImage generates srcset, defers loading off the critical path, and guards against layout shift. Two rules catch people out: you must give width and height unless you use fill, and you must not give both - using fill with width or height throws a RuntimeError at runtime. A missing sizes attribute logs a warning in the dev server (it warns rather than fails the build), and placeholder is either a valueless attribute or a URL - the string blur is not valid on its own.

performance.question: A Material table with 500+ rows plus filtering and sorting is slow. How do you diagnose and fix it?
performance.answer: Measure first: open DevTools Performance while interacting, and look at how much time is script versus rendering, and how many DOM nodes exist. The usual causes are too many rows in the DOM, a filter or sort running on every change-detection cycle, and identity churn destroying and rebuilding rows. The fixes map one to one: render only visible rows with CdkVirtualScrollViewport and cdkVirtualFor, keep components OnPush, treat filter and sort as a debounced stream with switchMap so rapid typing collapses into one operation, give rows a stable trackBy so unchanged nodes are reused, and cache the comparator instead of allocating one per cycle. Past roughly 10k rows, filter and sort on the server and virtualize the results.

examples.title: Virtual scroll - only the visible rows exist
examples.code:
{{ row.name }} — {{ row.amount }}
trackId = (_: number, r: Row) => r.id; // stable identity
examples.explanation: 500 rows become ~10 DOM nodes; trackBy lets Angular reuse nodes across sort and filter.

examples.title: Filter and sort as a debounced stream
examples.explanation: One request per settled query instead of one per keystroke; the comparator is computed once per sort change.

performance.question: What caching strategies do you use in a front-end application?
performance.answer: There are several layers, and a good answer names which one solves which problem. The browser HTTP cache (Cache-Control: max-age, immutable, plus ETag revalidation) and a CDN edge cache are for static assets and GET responses you control; content-hashed filenames (main.abc123.js) let you cache them forever and bust the cache on deploy. A service worker (Angular's built-in ngsw or Workbox) adds a layer independent of the network with runtime strategies: cache-first for static assets, network-first for fresh data, and stale-while-revalidate when you want a fast render plus a background refresh. Inside the running app you cache in memory: an HTTP interceptor or a shareReplay'd observable deduplicates and shares one request across components, and a signals store (or NgRx entity) keeps already-loaded data so a route transition does not refetch. Persistence (localStorage, IndexedDB) survives reloads for things like a user profile or a feature list. The hard part is invalidation, not storage: version your cache keys, prefer stale-while-revalidate over a long max-age for data, never cache authenticated responses in shared caches, and always keep a path to force a refresh. Without an invalidation story a cache just makes bugs look intermittent.

examples.title: HTTP cache headers: immutable assets vs revalidated data
examples.explanation: Hashed assets can be immutable because the name changes with the content; data uses ETag so an unchanged response comes back as a 304 instead of a full body.

examples.title: Share one in-flight request across components (shareReplay)
examples.explanation: Every caller after the first subscribes to the same underlying request instead of firing another one; swap in a signal store or Workbox runtime caching for the persisted layer.

performance.question: What do you actually change to make an Angular application faster?
performance.answer: I start by naming where the time goes, because every bottleneck is one of five things - network, main-thread work, rendering volume, bundle size or memory - and each has a different fix. Network: cut redundant requests before anything else, by debouncing input, dropping duplicates and only asking for what the screen shows; a 900ms API call dwarfs any template optimisation. Main thread: run OnPush everywhere, keep template expressions trivial by moving work into computed signals, and avoid deep change-detection passes. Rendering volume: render only what is on screen with pagination or virtual scrolling, and let track() in @for reuse DOM instead of rebuilding it. Bundle: lazy-load features with loadComponent, audit what the initial chunk actually contains, and drop dependencies that tree shaking cannot remove. Then the hygiene items: compress images and fonts, measure with Lighthouse and Angular DevTools rather than guessing, and verify before and after with the same profile. Most wins come from removing work, not from making work faster - and the last 10 per cent is rarely worth the readability it costs.

examples.title: The search pipeline that removes most wasted work
examples.explanation: One request per pause instead of one per keystroke, no request for a repeat query, stale responses cancelled, and nothing left subscribed after destroy. Four lines that usually beat any micro-optimisation.

performance.question: How would you put together a performance report for an application?
performance.answer: A report answers one question - is it fast, for whom, and what is the next thing to fix - so I structure it as baseline, evidence, prioritised findings, then retest. Baseline: Core Web Vitals from real users (LCP for first paint, INP for responsiveness, CLS for stability) rather than only lab numbers, plus the environment they came from. Evidence: Lighthouse for the lab run, WebPageTest for filmstrips and connection conditions, Chrome DevTools and Angular DevTools for long tasks and expensive change detection, and bundle analysis for who is owning each kilobyte. Findings are written as a list ordered by impact against effort, each with the measurement, the suspected cause, the fix, an owner and how we will know it worked - for example the reports route ships a 410 kB chunk because a CSV exporter is bundled into it, fixed by a dynamic import, verified by re-running the build. Numbers are compared before and after under the same conditions, because a green Lighthouse score on office wifi tells you almost nothing about a user on a train. Budgets then keep it honest: bundle budgets fail the build, so the report becomes a threshold rather than a slide.

examples.title: What a finding looks like
examples.code:
Finding: first load is 8.1s on Slow 4G (LCP 5.4s, target <= 2.5s)
Cause:   640 kB of initial JS, 210 kB of it unused on the landing route
Fix:     lazy-load the reports + admin features, drop the moment.js locale bundle
Owner:   frontend
Verify:  ng build budget pass, Lighthouse CI run on the PR, RUM LCP for 7 days
examples.explanation: Every line is checkable: a number someone can reproduce, a cause someone can confirm, and a verification that does not rely on feeling faster.

rxjs.question: What is an Observable in RxJS and how is it different from a Promise?
rxjs.answer: An Observable is lazy, cold by default, and can emit multiple values over time; it supports cancellation via unsubscribe() and is composable with operators. A Promise is eager, emits at most one value, is not cancellable, and is not pipeable. For example: new Observable(sub => { interval(1000).subscribe(n => sub.next(n)); return () => clear(); }) emits many values and can be torn down, while fetch() returns a single-value Promise. A Promise is either pending, fulfilled or rejected and settles exactly once, and async/await is sugar over its then() chain; an Observable may emit many times, may be cancelled, and is pipeable into every operator RxJS has. Reach for a Promise when the result is a single event you will wait for, and for an Observable when it is a stream you may need to cancel, throttle or combine - Angular's HttpClient returns Observables precisely so an unsubscribe can cancel an in-flight request.

examples.title: Observable vs Promise
examples.explanation: Observable emits over time and teardown is explicit; Promise settles once.

rxjs.question: What is the difference between cold and hot Observables?
rxjs.answer: A cold Observable produces its values inside the subscription (each subscriber gets its own producer/sequence) — e.g., HTTP calls via HttpClient are cold. A hot Observable shares a single producer among subscribers (late subscribers may miss values) — e.g., a DOM event or a Subject/ConnectableObservable. You can convert cold to hot using share(), shareReplay(), publish()/connect(), or multicast().

examples.title: Cold vs hot
examples.explanation: Cold = per-subscriber producer; hot = shared producer.

rxjs.question: What is a Subject, how does it differ from a plain Observable, and when would you use BehaviorSubject, ReplaySubject or AsyncSubject?
rxjs.answer: A plain Observable is unicast: each subscriber triggers its own independent execution of the producer, so it cannot share one stream between consumers. A Subject is a special type of Observable that is also an Observer: values are pushed into it with next(), and it multicasts that same stream to every subscriber at once, which is how a single data source is shared across an app. Subject: multicast, no initial value, subscribers only get values emitted after subscribing (useful for event buses). BehaviorSubject: requires an initial value, emits the current value to new subscribers (useful for shared auth/user state). ReplaySubject(bufferSize): replays a fixed number of past values to new subscribers (useful for caching chat history). AsyncSubject: emits only the last value and only on completion (useful for one-shot async results).

examples.title: BehaviorSubject
examples.explanation: BehaviorSubject emits current value to new subscribers.

rxjs.question: When should you use combineLatest, forkJoin, withLatestFrom, and merge?
rxjs.answer: combineLatest: emits when any source emits, after all have emitted at least once — combine related live values (filters + list). forkJoin: emits once, only after all complete with their last value — parallel one-shot requests that all must finish. withLatestFrom: emits only when the source emits, combining the latest values from others (primary stream drives). merge: concurrently emits values from multiple observables as they arrive (union of event streams).

examples.title: combineLatest vs forkJoin
examples.explanation: combineLatest stays live; forkJoin is one-shot on completion.

examples.title: withLatestFrom and merge
examples.explanation: withLatestFrom emits only when the source emits (the others must have emitted at least once); merge just forwards everything as it arrives.

rxjs.question: What is switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap, and exhaustMap? Give an example for each.
rxjs.answer: switchMap: cancels the previous inner observable on a new outer emission — typeahead/search (cancel stale requests). mergeMap (flatMap): subscribes to all inner observables in parallel, emits results as they come — independent parallel calls. concatMap: subscribes sequentially, waits for current inner to complete before next — queued operations (saving drafts in order). exhaustMap: ignores new outer emissions while the current inner is active — login/save button mash prevention.

examples.title: switchMap vs exhaustMap (search vs save)
examples.explanation: switchMap cancels previous inner on new outer; exhaustMap drops outer while inner is active.

examples.title: Further reading
examples.code: https://blog.angular-university.io/rxjs-higher-order-mapping/
examples.explanation: A detailed walkthrough of the higher-order mapping operators and when each one is the right choice.

rxjs.question: What is the purpose of share(), shareReplay(), and refCount()?
rxjs.answer: share() turns a cold observable hot and replays the source among subscribers; refCount() keeps it alive only while there is >=1 subscriber (unsubscribes upstream when zero). shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true/false }) caches recent values for late subscribers and controls whether it stays alive when no subscribers exist — often used to cache HTTP responses. Use refCount carefully to avoid re-triggering a cold source unexpectedly.

examples.title: shareReplay
examples.explanation: Caches last emission for late subscribers; refCount controls lifecycle.

rxjs.question: How do you prevent memory leaks when subscribing to Observables?
rxjs.answer: Prefer the async pipe in templates (auto-unsubscribes on destroy). For imperative code, unsubscribe() in ngOnDestroy, or use takeUntil() with a destroy Subject, takeUntilDestroyed() (Angular 16+), first(), take(1), or finalize(). Also avoid long-lived global subscriptions without cleanup. For toSignal(), subscriptions are tied to the injection context (DestroyRef) automatically.

examples.title: takeUntilDestroyed
examples.code:
import { takeUntilDestroyed } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';
fromEvent(window, 'resize').pipe(takeUntilDestroyed()).subscribe(...);
examples.explanation: Auto-cleans up when injection context is destroyed.

rxjs.question: What is the difference between map, tap, switchMap and exhaustMap in terms of what they return?
rxjs.answer: map: transforms values, returns the same stream type (value -> value). tap (do): side effect only, returns the same observable unchanged (use for logging). switchMap: maps outer value to an inner observable and flattens it, emitting values from the latest inner (projects to Observable). exhaustMap: maps to an inner observable but ignores outer emissions while inner is active (projects to Observable).

examples.title: tap vs map
examples.explanation: tap does not transform values; map projects them.

rxjs.question: Give a small example of debouncing a search input with RxJS.
rxjs.answer: In a component: fromEvent(this.input.nativeElement, 'input').pipe(debounceTime(300), distinctUntilChanged(), switchMap(q => this.service.search(q)), takeUntilDestroyed()).subscribe(results => this.results.set(results)). This waits 300ms after typing stops, skips duplicates, cancels stale requests on new input, and cleans up on destroy.

examples.title: Search debounce
examples.explanation: Debounce, ignore duplicates, cancel stale requests.

rxjs.question: What is error handling in RxJS and when would you use catchError, retry, and retry with a delay?
rxjs.answer: catchError: catches an error in the stream and returns a replacement Observable (a fallback value, EMPTY, or a retry attempt) so the stream can carry on. retry(n): re-subscribes immediately up to n times - fine for a single transient blip. retry({ delay }): the modern form, where delay can be a number, a function of the error and retry index (that is how you do exponential backoff), or an observable such as timer(1000). Note that retryWhen() is deprecated in RxJS 7 - reach for retry({ delay }) instead. Handle errors close to where they can be meaningfully recovered, and remember that catchError replaces the stream, so anything downstream of it will not see the failure unless you re-throw. In a real service I classify before I rethrow: status 0 is network or CORS, 401 means re-authenticate, 403 means authenticated but not allowed, 404 is a contract problem and 5xx is upstream, and each deserves a different log or reaction; loading state is cleared in finalize() so the screen cannot end up stuck half-finished. The rule to remember is that catchError must return an Observable - hand back fallback data such as of([]) when the view can degrade to an empty state, or throwError(() => error) when the caller has to decide.

examples.title: retry with backoff
examples.explanation: Custom retry with exponential backoff before failing. retryWhen(errors => errors.pipe(delay(...))) is the deprecated equivalent.

rxjs.question: What do debounceTime and distinctUntilChanged each do, and why would you use them together?
rxjs.answer: They solve different problems, which is why they are complementary rather than interchangeable. debounceTime(duration) waits for silence: it emits the most recent value only after no new value has arrived for that period, so a user typing 'angular' in half a second produces one emission instead of six. throttleTime(duration) is the opposite temperament - it emits immediately, then suppresses everything for the interval, which suits high-frequency sources where the latest value matters less than a steady one. distinctUntilChanged() does no timing at all: it compares each emission with the previous one and drops the repeat, with a custom comparator available when equality is not what you mean. In a search box the pair covers two different kinds of waste: debounceTime stops the request per keystroke, and distinctUntilChanged stops a request when the query came back to a value you already asked for - typing, pausing, deleting a trailing space and retyping it should not cost a second round trip. Then switchMap does the third job, cancelling the response you no longer want. Chain them in that order - quieten the stream, drop repeats, then flatten with cancellation - because debounceTime after switchMap would still leave stale responses free to land.

examples.title: The standard search chain, with what each stage buys
examples.explanation: Three operators, three costs removed: request volume, duplicate requests, and wasted responses. None of them can do the other two jobs.

signals.question: What is a Signal and how is it different from an RxJS Observable?
signals.answer: A Signal is a synchronous, granular reactive primitive: a value you read by calling it (count()) and update with set/update, that automatically notifies consumers that depend on it. An Observable is an asynchronous, lazy stream you must subscribe to, with operators for retry, debounce and merging. Signals are ideal for component-local and synchronous UI state; Observables stay the tool for async event streams, HTTP and WebSockets. You bridge the two with toObservable() and toSignal().

examples.title: signal() basic read/write
examples.explanation: Read with () and update via set/update; computed derives reactively.

signals.question: When would you use signals instead of observables, and can signals replace RxJS completely?
signals.answer: Use signals when the state is synchronous UI state - selection, toggles, count, a view model - where you want direct value access without the async pipe or subscriptions. Do not try to replace RxJS for genuinely async work like HTTP retries, websockets, or streams that need cancellation and composition. In an interview, the framing is: streams feed signals, signals feed the template - the correct architecture composes both rather than picking one.

examples.title: When to use signals
examples.explanation: Synchronous UI state → signals; async/event streams → RxJS.

signals.question: What are computed signals and effects, and when do you use each?
signals.answer: computed() creates a read-only derived signal that lazily recalculates only when its dependencies change - use it for anything you can derive (total = price() * qty()). effect() runs a side effect whenever the signals it reads change - use it only when you have no reactive alternative: syncing with a non-reactive library, analytics, DOM APIs. It should never be your first choice because it runs as a scheduled pass after change detection rather than at the point of the write, it runs at least once on creation, and it re-runs on every change.

examples.title: computed vs effect
examples.explanation: computed is read-only derived; effect is for external side effects.

signals.question: What is the diamond problem in Observables, and why doesn't it occur with signals?
signals.answer: When two or more derived streams share a common source and are combined, RxJS can glitch - combineLatest emitting multiple times for what is logically one update. Signals are synchronous and batched: if you update two source signals, a computed or effect depending on both recalculates once per batch, not per dependency. That single recalc per write cycle is why signal graphs avoid the duplicate-emission problem.

examples.title: Batching intuition
examples.explanation: Synchronous updates batch → computed/effect run once per batch.

signals.question: When do you need untracked() inside an effect?
signals.answer: untracked() removes dependency tracking inside an effect. You need it when an effect reads signals it should not subscribe to - for example reading a value to send to a server or to focus an element, where you do not want the effect to re-run when that value changes. A common failure is an effect that reads several signals and also writes to one, so writes would retrigger it forever; wrapping the write in untracked() breaks the loop.

examples.title: untracked() to avoid loops
examples.explanation: Prevents the effect from re-running when log changes.

signals.question: How would you plan a migration from an Angular 12 app that uses RxJS to Signals?
signals.answer: Plan incrementally instead of a big-bang rewrite. Start with component-local UI state and convert @Input/@Output to signal inputs (input()) so computed() can replace ngOnChanges. Then convert simple BehaviorSubject state in services to signal()/state, leaving HTTP and async pipelines on RxJS. Use the dev tools, keep the graph acyclic (never effect + set()), and rely on the signal-input-migration schematic for automation before touching complex features.

examples.title: ngOnChanges -> computed (the mechanical swap)
examples.explanation: computed replaces ngOnChanges entirely: no manual flag, no stale branch when only one input is set.

examples.title: BehaviourSubject -> signal in a service
examples.explanation: Derived flags become computeds; consumers read store.user() directly instead of the async pipe.

examples.title: Keep RxJS for async, feed it into signals
examples.explanation: The request stays an observable; only the view-facing state becomes a signal.

signals.question: Are NgOnInit and ngOnChanges still needed in a fully signal-based application?
signals.answer: Largely no. ngOnChanges is replaced by signal inputs (input()) combined with computed() - derived values recalculate reactively instead of in a hook. NgOnInit mostly becomes unnecessary since you can read signals and start effects inline; data fetching moves into resource()/rxResource(). The lifecycle hooks still exist and remain useful for view concerns like afterNextRender, but the signal-based APIs remove most of the boilerplate they forced.

examples.title: Lifecycle shift
examples.explanation: Many init cases move to inline reads/effects instead of NgOnInit.

signals.question: What is linkedSignal, and why is calling set() inside an effect() considered an anti-pattern?
signals.answer: linkedSignal creates a writable signal that is linked to a source signal and resets to the source value when the source changes - ideal for a filter dropdown whose selection must reset when the underlying list changes. Writing signal.set() inside an effect() to do the same thing is an anti-pattern because it writes a signal being read by the effect, creating a feedback loop; Angular warns about it in dev mode. Use linkedSignal when the derived value must be writable, and computed() when it must not.

examples.title: Overload 1 - source only (resets to the derived value)
examples.explanation: With no computation, the linked value resets to the source's current derived value.

examples.title: Overload 2 - source + computation (recompute on source change, keep local edits)
examples.explanation: With a computation you control the reset rule - here 'keep previous unless the source really changed'.

examples.title: The anti-pattern this replaces
examples.explanation: linkedSignal expresses 'derived but writable' declaratively, with no feedback loop.

signals.question: How can you replace BehaviorSubject and Subject with signals?
signals.answer: A BehaviorSubject is really two things: it always holds a current value, and it notifies subscribers when that value changes. signal() covers exactly that: signal(0) has an initial value, you read it with count(), and you change it with set() or update(). Because signals are pull-based and synchronous, a template reads them directly, a computed() derives new values from them, and an effect() reacts to changes, all with no subscription to create and therefore no leak to manage. Where the mapping is not exact is a plain Subject, which is a stream of events with no current value. If the thing always has a latest value, use a signal; if it is a stream of many events or you need RxJS operators (debounce, buffer, retry), keep the Subject, because signals are state, not a stream, and cannot be composed with operators. You can also bridge the two: toSignal() wraps an Observable as a signal, and toObservable() turns a signal into an Observable. In practice an injectable service exposes a private writable signal and a public readonly signal, which replaces the BehaviorSubject-in-a-service pattern outright.

examples.title: BehaviorSubject vs signal
examples.explanation: The signal replaces the value-plus-notification pair; the readonly view replaces asObservable(), and derived values come from computed() instead of subscribe().

examples.title: Bridging with toSignal / toObservable
examples.explanation: Use toSignal when a signal is the right consumer, and toObservable when you still need RxJS operators; the two models interoperate rather than compete.

signals.question: A filter in a toolbar and a list in a distant component must stay in sync. Show how signals replace the BehaviorSubject service.
signals.answer: This is the classic shared-service problem: two components that are not parent and child need to read and write the same state. The old pattern put a BehaviorSubject in an injectable, called next() on change, and had every consumer subscribe and remember to unsubscribe. With signals the same service holds the state as a signal, exposes a readonly copy, and offers a method to change it; components read the signal in their template or derive from it with computed(), so there is no subscription and no initial-value plumbing. Because the signal is the single source of truth, the list can compute its filtered rows from it directly. If a consumer needs to run a side effect rather than derive a value, use an effect(); if it only displays or derives, computed() is enough. The one rule that carries over is ownership: one service owns the state, and the components do not hold their own copies of it.

examples.title: Before: BehaviorSubject service
examples.explanation: Works, but every consumer subscribes, has to unsubscribe (often on destroy), and the initial value is implicit in the subject's constructor.

examples.title: After: one signal, read directly by both components
examples.explanation: The toolbar writes and the list derives; computed() re-runs only when the signal it reads changes, so the two components stay in sync with no manual subscription.

signals.question: What are toSignal and toObservable, and when would you use each?
signals.answer: toSignal and toObservable both live in @angular/core/rxjs-interop and are the bridge between the two reactivity models. toSignal() turns an Observable into a signal: it subscribes for you, sinks the latest emission into the signal, and - because creation is tracked in an injection context - unsubscribes automatically via DestroyRef when the consumer is destroyed. Pass initialValue so reads before the first emission are something other than undefined. toObservable() goes the other way: it turns a signal into an Observable that emits the current value immediately to new subscribers (like a BehaviorSubject) and then every change; it also tears down when destroyed. Use toSignal() when templates or a computed() read state, which is the common case of handing an HttpClient or a router/Subject stream to a signal-based template. Use toObservable() when you still need RxJS operators - debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged, switchMap, combineLatest - over a signal's changes, or when a component must consume an Observable. Neither replaces the other, and the signal-first answer reaches for them at boundaries: most state should be signals and computed(), and the bridges exist so RxJS streams can be consumed or fed where the other model is already in play.

examples.title: Observable -> signal with toSignal
examples.explanation: Pass initialValue so the signal is not undefined before the first emission; the subscription and its cleanup are handled by the injection context (DestroyRef).

examples.title: signal -> Observable with toObservable
examples.explanation: toObservable emits the current value immediately to new subscribers (like a BehaviorSubject) and every change after that, which is exactly when you want debounce or switchMap over a signal's history.

misc.question: What is AOT vs JIT compilation?
misc.answer: JIT compiles Angular templates and decorators at runtime in the browser, while AOT compiles them ahead-of-time during the build. AOT is the default today: it catches template errors at build time, runs faster in the browser, and ships less runtime compiler code.

examples.title: AOT vs JIT at runtime
examples.explanation: AOT shifts compilation to the build step: smaller runtime bundle, faster startup, template errors caught in CI.

misc.question: What is a standalone component?
misc.answer: A standalone component is one that does not belong to an NgModule: it declares its own imports, services, pipes and directives directly in its imports array. Since Angular 19 standalone is the default for new apps and makes lazy-loading routes with loadComponent straightforward.

examples.title: Standalone is just an imports array
examples.explanation: No NgModule to register: dependencies are declared on the component itself, which is what makes loadComponent lazy routes trivial.

misc.question: What is CORS, and why does a browser block cross-origin requests?
misc.answer: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is a browser mechanism that decides whether JavaScript running on one origin (scheme plus host plus port) may read a response from another. It exists because of the same-origin policy: by default a page can send requests to other origins (images, CSS, fonts) but its JavaScript cannot read the responses, so a malicious site cannot silently exfiltrate data from a bank API while the user is logged in. CORS is the negotiated exception. For a simple request (GET/POST/HEAD using default headers) the response headers alone decide; as soon as custom headers, methods like PUT/DELETE, or credentials are involved, the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request asking which origins, methods and headers the server allows, and only ships the real request if the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Allow-Methods, -Allow-Headers and -Allow-Credentials. Crucially, CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server: the blocked request still reaches and runs on the server; only the response is withheld from your code. In an Angular app the everyday symptom is the API not sending the right headers, or sending the wrong origin. In development you sidestep it with the CLI's proxy (proxy.conf.json) so the browser only ever talks to the same origin; in production the backend or an API gateway must set the headers instead.

examples.title: The preflight flow
examples.explanation: Custom methods, headers or credentials force a preflight; the real request is sent only if the OPTIONS response approves it. The server still sees the blocked request - CORS never stops it from arriving.

examples.title: Avoid it in dev with the Angular proxy
examples.explanation: The dev server proxies /api calls server-side, so the browser never performs a cross-origin request; in production the backend or an API gateway must set the CORS headers instead.

examples.title: Further reading
examples.code: CORS in 100 Seconds - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PNtFSVU-YTI
examples.explanation: A short visual walkthrough of the same-origin policy, preflight and the response headers.

misc.question: What is Agile, and what does a sprint actually look like day to day?
misc.answer: Agile is an approach, not a ceremony: deliver in small increments, get them in front of real users, and let what you learn change the next increment instead of defending a plan written a year ago. Scrum is the most common framework for putting that into a calendar. The product owner owns and orders the backlog and answers what is worth building; the development team owns how and delivers it; the scrum master owns the process and the impediments. The sprint is a fixed box - usually one or two weeks - with four events: planning to agree a goal and take the top of the backlog into the sprint, a daily scrum to inspect and adjust rather than to report status, a review where the increment is demonstrated to stakeholders and feedback changes the backlog, and a retrospective about how the team worked. Underneath sits the Definition of Done - the shared bar for what complete means: reviewed, tests green, accessibility checked, deployed to staging, accepted. As the Angular developer on it I take a story, clarify the acceptance criteria with the analyst, estimate it with the team, build the UI and the services, write tests, raise a pull request, address review comments and support QA through to release. For an employee-search feature I would split it into the search form, the API integration, loading and empty states, accessibility and automated tests - small enough to review in one sitting and to ship independently.

examples.title: Splitting one feature into reviewable increments
examples.code:
Story: As a recruiter I can search employees by name and department

Slice 1  search form + validation, no data          (shippable, shows the UX)
Slice 2  GET integration + loading / empty states   (usable end to end)
Slice 3  error and retry states + no-results copy   (polish that QA can test)
Slice 4  keyboard + screen-reader pass, axe in CI   (Definition of Done)
Slice 5  debounce, cancel stale requests, tests     (performance, measured)
examples.explanation: Each slice leaves the application in a working, demoable state, so feedback on the design arrives after slice 1 instead of after the whole feature is built.

misc.question: What is the difference between Scrum and Kanban, and what are story points, velocity and the Definition of Done?
misc.answer: Both are ways of working empirically, but they optimise for different shapes of work. Scrum is a fixed cadence: roles, a timeboxed sprint, a committed sprint goal, and no mid-sprint changes, which suits work you can plan a week or two ahead. Kanban is continuous flow: you visualise work on a board, limit work in progress so the team finishes rather than starts, and pull the next item when capacity frees up, which suits a stream of support, incident and bug work that does not fit a sprint. Kanban measures cycle time - how long one item takes from start to finish - while Scrum measures velocity. Story points are a relative estimate of effort, complexity and uncertainty, typically on a Fibonacci scale; they are not hours and not a commitment, and the moment a point target is set for a person it stops being useful. Velocity is the average number of points a team completes per sprint - a planning signal for how much a future sprint can hold, never a performance metric. The Definition of Done is different again: it is the shared, non-negotiable criteria for what complete means (code reviewed, pipeline green, accessibility checked, deployed, accepted), as opposed to the acceptance criteria of an individual story, which say what that story must do. In interviews I keep that distinction crisp, because DoD-versus-acceptance-criteria is a common follow-up.

examples.title: The four things, side by side
examples.code:
Scrum        fixed sprint, roles, events, sprint goal; measures velocity
Kanban       continuous pull, WIP limits, no sprints; measures cycle time
Story point   relative size of ONE item (1, 2, 3, 5, 8...) - not hours
Velocity      average points completed per sprint - a forecasting signal, not a target
Definition   shared bar for every item: reviewed, tested, accessible,
 of Done       deployed to staging, accepted
Acceptance    the contract for ONE story: what this change must do
examples.explanation: Points size an item, velocity forecasts a sprint, the Definition of Done gates every item - confusing any two of them is what makes estimates feel like commitments.

misc.question: What is the difference between prompting an AI model and using an AI coding agent?
misc.answer: Prompting is a single turn: you give a model an instruction and the context you think it needs, and you get text or code back that you then read, judge and apply yourself. 'Explain how switchMap differs from mergeMap' is prompting, and the model has no idea what your repository looks like. An agent is a loop around a model: it is given a goal plus tools - reading files, searching the codebase, editing, running the shell and the test suite - and it plans, acts, observes the result of each action, and iterates until the goal is met or it needs a decision from you. 'Find where duplicate employee-search requests originate in this project, fix them, run the tests and summarise the diff' is an agent task, and the difference is not just length: the agent's output depends on what it found, and it can verify its own work. That changes what good looks like. A good prompt states the objective, the relevant context, the constraints, the shape of the output and how you will judge it. A good agent setup adds scoped permissions, repository instructions it can follow, a single command that tells it whether it is done, and a git history that makes everything reversible. The bit I would not skip: an agent that can edit files is not an agent that is right. I review the diff, run the tests myself, and read security-sensitive changes line by line - the same scepticism as reviewing a colleague, with less benefit of the doubt.

examples.title: The same request at two levels
examples.code:
PROMPT (one turn, output you must apply)
"Give me an RxJS operator chain that debounces a search input and cancels stale requests."

AGENT (goal, tools, verification loop)
"In this project, find where typing in the employee search box issues a request per
keystroke. Change it so only one request is in flight and repeats are skipped, keep
existing tests passing, add a test for the new behaviour, and tell me which files
changed and why. Run `npx ng test` to verify."

// the agent reads, edits, runs the suite, reads the failure it caused, and fixes it
// before reporting back - the loop is the difference, not the model
examples.explanation: The prompt asks for knowledge; the agent is given an outcome plus a way to check it reached one. Everything else - permissions, review, reversibility - follows from that.

misc.question: How would you integrate Claude into an application, and what are the main challenges?
misc.answer: I would never call the provider from the browser. The Angular app talks to our own backend, the backend validates the user, permissions and input, holds the API key in a secrets manager, calls the model, validates the response against the shape the UI needs, and returns it - so the key never ships in a bundle and every call is accounted for. The UI then does what UIs are good at: streaming output as it arrives, a visible loading and cancelled state, an obvious way to edit or discard what came back, and never auto-executing a consequential action on the model's say-so. The challenges are consistent enough to recite: hallucination, mitigated by grounding answers in retrieved data, validating structured output against a schema, and a human in the loop for anything that matters; prompt injection, mitigated by treating user input and retrieved content strictly as data, keeping instructions in a separate trusted layer, and giving tools the least privilege that works; latency, mitigated by streaming, timeouts and background jobs for long work; cost and rate limits, mitigated by quotas, caching of repeated requests and token budgets with monitoring; privacy, mitigated by minimising what leaves - no secrets, no personal data you do not need, no prompt logging that becomes a compliance problem; and reliability, mitigated by retrying only the retryable (429 and 5xx), a fallback behaviour when the model is unavailable, and a feature flag to switch the whole thing off. The last one matters more than people expect: you will want an off switch on day one.

examples.title: The flow, and what each hop is responsible for
examples.code:
browser                  your backend                    provider API
  |                          |                                |
  | POST /api/summarise      |                                |
  | { ticketId, locale }     |                                |
  |------------------------->| validate session + permissions  |
  |                          | check input size / rate limit   |
  |                          | read API key from secrets       |
  |                          |-------------------------------->|
  |                          |<-------------------------------|
  |                          | validate output against schema  |
  |<-------------------------| log metadata only (no prompt)   |
  | SSE stream of tokens     |                                |

Angular side: post to your own endpoint, stream with fromEvent/fetch SSM,
surface loading / error / cancel, and require a human to accept the result.
examples.explanation: Every risk is answered at one of these hops: key exposure by never leaving the backend, injection by where instructions live, cost by the quota before the call, privacy by what you put on the wire at all.

misc.question: What is the difference between AG Grid's client-side and server-side row models?
misc.answer: They differ in one question: where does sorting, filtering and grouping happen. The client-side row model loads the whole dataset into the browser and the grid does the work - sort, filter, group, aggregate, paginate - which makes every interaction instant and needs no server contract, and it is the right choice while the data fits comfortably in memory: thousands to low hundreds of thousands of rows, virtualised so only visible rows exist in the DOM. Past that point the browser is paying for data nobody will look at, and you move to the server-side row model: the grid keeps only the rows in view and asks a datasource for them as the user sorts, filters, groups or scrolls, sending the full request context (start row, sort model, filter model, group state) so the server can answer authoritatively. That buys you millions of rows and server-owned business rules, and costs you an API that understands all of it, careful cancellation of superseded requests, a caching strategy, and loading states in the UI. AG Grid also ships an infinite row model for append-only paging and a viewport model for sparse data such as maps, and the server-side model is an enterprise feature while the client-side one is free. My decision inputs: dataset size, whether the rules for filtering and grouping must live server-side, backend capability, and how much offline or instant interaction you need.

examples.title: What the server-side datasource has to implement
examples.explanation: The grid hands you a page plus the whole sort and filter state, and expects success or fail - which is where cancellation of stale requests and a sensible loading state become your problem rather than the grid's.

behavioural.question: Which behavioural question framework will you use to answer these questions?
behavioural.answer:
This is often the first question of the loop, and it is a free opportunity either
way. Weak answers name STAR and stop, or worse, explain that they do not use a
framework because they answer honestly. Good answers name a small toolkit and match
the tool to the shape of the question, because the frameworks differ in which
specific weakness they defend against. Say which one you would choose for a given
question, and why, and it sounds deliberate rather than recited.

examples.title: The toolkit and when to use it
examples.code:
STAR
Situation, Task, Action, Result. The default for a past action.

STAR-L
STAR plus Learnings. The added beat is the point: it forces a reflection step
STAR skips, which is usually the most interesting part of your answer.

CARL
Challenge, Action, Result, Lesson. Obstacle-first rather than context-first, so
the difficulty leads instead of hiding at the end. Useful when the hardest part
was the problem itself.

SPSIL
Situation, Problem, Solution, Impact, Lessons. Developed by IGotAnOffer as a
STAR alternative. It splits STAR's blurry Task and Action into a clearer
Problem and Solution, and makes the Lesson step non-optional.

SOAR
Situation, Obstacle, Action, Result. Same family as CARL, used where the
obstacle is the interesting part.

PAR
Point, Example, Reason, Point. For questions that are really opinion rather
than story.

PREP
Point, Reason, Example, Point. For philosophy questions - why should we hire
you, how do you decide what to optimise for.

PSB
Problem, Solution, Benefit. For hypotheticals, where there is no real past
event to draw on.

SBI
Situation, Behaviour, Impact. For feedback you gave to someone else. Avoid the
compliment sandwich - the person cannot tell what to change.
examples.explanation:
Matching the framework to the question type, and using STAR-L or SPSIL when a
learning beat is what the question is really after, is the signal. A framework
recital with no matching is what fails.

behavioural.question: Tell me about yourself.
behavioural.answer:
The most under-prepared question in the loop, and the one where most people
either recite a resume chronologically or start with their university. It is
not a life story - it is a 60 to 90 second argument for why this conversation is
worth having, ending where this role begins. The structure that works: present
tense and current role, the two or three things you are actually good at
backed by a concrete outcome each, then the bridge into why this role. A good
tell is naming what you want next, because that frames the rest of the loop.
Keep it under 90 seconds so there is time for them to ask. Two traps to avoid: nothing from before your professional life - university, school and hobbies do not belong in this answer, because the interviewer already has your resume and is not asking you to read it back to them - and nothing negative about your current or previous employer, since they will reasonably assume you will describe them the same way in six months. Whatever you claim, expect it to become the next question: pick two or three things you can go an inch deeper on, each with a number and a story attached, and steer towards them instead of listing ten you cannot defend.

examples.title: 60 to 90 seconds, ending at this role
examples.code:
BAD
Graduated from X in 2015, then interned at A, then joined B as a frontend
developer, then moved to C...
- Chronological, no point, and the interviewer now has your resume in front
  of them.

GOOD
I am a frontend engineer at C, where I own our Angular design system and the
checkout flow.

Two things I would say I am genuinely good at. First, I cut initial bundle
size by 180kb on checkout last year - mostly by auditing what was actually
being composed rather than swapping libraries - and I left a CI budget behind
so it stayed down. Second, I have led three version migrations end to end, and
the last one was a major upgrade across four teams where the useful part was
agreeing the sequencing with people who disagreed with me.

What I want next is to be closer to the whole system rather than one surface of
it, which is why this role interested me.
examples.explanation:
Ends at this role, has two concrete outcomes, and states what you want next so
the rest of the loop has a frame.

examples.title: The preparation that happens before you say a word
examples.code:
BEFORE THE ROUND
- Replace every generic line with your real domain and one number you can defend:
  what got faster, what shipped, what you owned. 'Improved performance' is not an answer.
- Treat every sentence as a potential next question: list the technologies you mention
  and be ready with a short answer for each of them.
- Keep it to 60-90 seconds. The opener's job is to choose your follow-ups, not to prove
  everything at once.
- Notice period, location and compensation are their questions to ask - do not fold
  logistics into the one answer you get to frame the conversation.
- Say it out loud once. A script recited from memory sounds like a script.
examples.explanation: The opener is a framing device: it decides what they ask next, so the follow-ups get prepared as deliberately as the answer itself.

behavioural.question: Walk me through your resume.
behavioural.answer:
Expectation-setting is the graded part: they want to know how you think and
where your story has gaps, not the contents. Narrate around two or three
threads rather than going chronologically, and be the one who names the gaps
first - a reorg, a short tenure, a gap, a pivot - because that reads as
self-awareness rather than being caught on it. For each thread say the problem,
your role, and the outcome. Do not narrate every job; if you have five, explain
what changed between them.

examples.title: Two threads, gaps named by you
examples.code:
Frame it as threads, not jobs:
- Thread 1: performance work. What the problem was, which parts were mine,
  what changed.
- Thread 2: migrations and cross-team delivery. Same structure.
- Then: the bits that do not fit, named by me first.

Naming a gap yourself
"She will ask about the 8 months at D, so say it first:
That was a reorg. My role was made redundant, and looking back I waited about
two months before looking externally, which cost me savings. I would handle
that differently - start while still employed."

Five jobs, one explanation
"I have had five jobs. Three were contract, which is why it looks like a lot:
two were three-month pieces, and between them I was in one bad agency that
placed me badly and I should have left sooner."
examples.explanation:
Gaps and churn named by you first is the entire tell. Chronological narration is
what loses this question.

behavioural.question: What is one weakness of yours?
behavioural.answer:
The scoring is entirely in which weakness you choose and whether the evidence
shows you worked on it. The three failing categories: a humblebrag disguised as
a strength, a weakness that is actually someone else's problem (my manager is
micromanaging), and a real weakness with no evidence of any attempt to fix it.
What works is a genuine, job-relevant weakness with a specific mitigation you
put in place, and ideally a story of it failing before the mitigation existed.
Pick something that is real and small enough that the fix is believable - you
cannot claim to have fixed chronic disorganisation, but you can describe a
system you built to stop losing context.

examples.title: Real, job-relevant, with the fix
examples.code:
BAD
I work too hard.
- Humblebrag. Everyone says this and it reads as having not prepared.

BAD
My previous manager was difficult to work with.
- Not your weakness, and you have just told them how you handle conflict.

BAD
I am not very good at saying no.
- Plausible but unevidenced, so it becomes a prediction they will test.

GOOD
I used to lose track of context when I came back to a thread after a day on
something else, and I would re-derive decisions that had already been made.

What it looked like: a task that had been scoped on Monday would be re-scoped
on Wednesday by me, with no memory of why the first answer was chosen.

What I changed: decisions that affect more than one person now get a two-line
written rationale - the problem, the choice, the rejected option. I do it at the
end of the day it is made, which takes about a minute.

Where it has not worked: for genuinely throwaway work I still skip it, and
occasionally that bites.
examples.explanation:
Real and job-relevant, a specific system rather than willpower, and an honest
note on where it still fails.

behavioural.question: Where do you see yourself in five years?
behavioural.answer:
Graded on whether it is compatible with the role rather than on the ambition. A
common failure is an answer that quietly exits - I want to run a team, or move
into product - which tells them you will leave. A technically strong answer
stays on the work, names a direction rather than a job title, and ties it to
something you have already shown you can do. Being vague is safer than being
wrong, but pure vagueness reads as no ambition. Aim for a direction, a reason it
suits you, and one honest uncertainty.

examples.title: Direction, not exit
examples.code:
BAD
I want to move into engineering management.
- Reads as a resignation letter with a two-year notice. Only use this if the
  role is on the management track and you say so explicitly.

BAD
I want to work somewhere more challenging.
- No direction at all.

GOOD
In five years I want to still be hands on, but owning the architecture of a
larger system than one surface - and to be the person who is trusted with the
hard technical judgement calls rather than just the tickets.

Why that direction: the part I am best at is the trade-off no one wants to
make, and I like that the work is not decided in advance. The engineering
management version of this is also a thing I want eventually, but it is a
different job and I would rather do it deliberately than drift into it.

The uncertainty: whether the next role gives me that scope. I would rather
choose it than wait for it.
examples.explanation:
Stays on the work, names a direction and a reason, and is honest about the
uncertainty instead of being either grandiose or evasive.

behavioural.question: Tell me about a project you are proud of.
behavioural.answer:
This is the most over-claimed question in the set, and the tell is a project
described in the plural - we, I - with no account of what you personally decided.
The strongest shape: pick a project where the interesting part was your
judgement, not the volume of work. Say what was hard about the decision, what you
chose, what you rejected, and what happened. Include a thing that went wrong or
something you would do differently, because an entirely flawless project reads as
either easy or rehearsed. Scale is not impressive; the decision is.

examples.title: One decision, one flaw
examples.code:
WEAK
We built a design system used by 40 teams.
- Team success, no personal decision, and the number is doing the work.

STRONG
Mine was the migration off a legacy build system. What makes it worth telling
about is a decision, not the work: we could have done it all at once, or
sequenced it by team.

I chose sequential, by dependency order rather than by team size or by which
team complained loudest. The argument against me was team size - the big teams
were still on the old pipeline for months and that hurt morale.

What it cost: about four months where the biggest teams had no path to the new
setup. I had predicted three.

The flaw: I did not budget for the two teams whose builds were not actually
independent, so we discovered mid-migration that the sequencing I had called
obvious was wrong for them. That was my analysis error, and it cost about three
weeks.

Result: zero rollbacks across 40 teams, and the sequencing doc was reused for
the platform migration afterwards.
examples.explanation:
One judgement call with a named alternative, a predicted cost, and a real
flaw that was yours. Scale is not the point.

behavioural.question: Tell me about a time you had to work in an area you knew nothing about.
behavioural.answer:
Graded on the method of getting competent, not on the subject matter - nobody
cares whether it was Kubernetes, a payments integration, or a regex. What they
are listening for is whether you found the people who knew, whether you made
your understanding explicit early enough to be corrected, and how you knew when
you were done. The move that raises the level is building a small thing early
and being visibly wrong in a low-risk place, because that is what actually
produces learning faster than reading.

examples.title: Learning by being visibly wrong, early
examples.code:
The area was our payments provider's webhook retry semantics. I knew nothing
about it.

Step one, cheap and fast: I asked three questions - which people actually know
this, what does a correct integration look like, and what is the most common way
people get it wrong. The third question was the valuable one, and it turned out
the standard advice was wrong for our case.

Step two: I wrote the naive integration first, against a sandbox, and it failed
in a way that confirmed the thing I had been told was fine. Cheap correction,
low stakes.

Step three: rather than keep guessing, I wrote down my model of the behaviour
as I understood it and sent it to the payments engineer to correct. She changed
two of my five assumptions and said the other three were right for reasons I had
not considered.

How I knew I was done: not when it felt clear, but when I could predict what the
system would do in the three cases we actually hit, and I had a test for each.
examples.explanation:
Asking what people commonly get wrong, testing cheap and early, and having an
explicit model that someone corrected - that is the method they are grading.

behavioural.question: Tell me about a time you simplified something complicated.
behavioural.answer:
Simplification is one of the highest-signal behaviours to demonstrate, and the
mistake is describing a cleanup as a simplification. A cleanup leaves the same
complexity with fewer lines. A simplification removes the complexity by changing
the model: you found that the requirement did not actually need generalising, or
you replaced a mechanism that had one use with direct code. Say what was
simplified, why the complicated version existed in the first place, and what
gave you the evidence to safely remove it.

examples.title: Removing the mechanism, not the lines
examples.code:
The trap
We refactored the validation module, removed 600 lines, and made it much
easier to read.
- A cleanup. Good, but not simplification.

The actual simplification
We had a generic form-validation engine: rules defined in JSON, a rule engine
that interpreted them, and a schema that had to stay in sync with the TypeScript
types.

It existed because two years earlier we thought we would need configurable
validation for two more teams.

What made it safe to remove: I grepped the rule definitions and found 41 of them,
and 38 were static. The other three were our login form and had not changed in
four months.

So we deleted the engine, inlined the 38 as typed functions so TypeScript now
checks them, and kept the three as three explicit validators. The JSON schema is
gone, so the class of bug where the two drifted cannot happen anymore.
